2026.MM43.1.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for Protective Tree Fencing in Yorkville Village - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
2026.MM43.1.s:
Yorkville Village is a highly valued tourist attraction whose shops, restaurants, and festivals also serve a dense residential area and the entire Toronto community.

In cooperation with the Bloor Yorkville Business Improvement Area, the city has installed 119 street trees in sidewalk pits on Bellair Street, Cumberland Street (west of Bay), Yorkville Avenue (west of Bay), Hazelton Avenue (from Yorkville to approximately 40 Hazelton), Scollard Street (west of Bay) and Bay Street (from St. Mary to just north of Scollard). The trees contribute significantly to the beauty of the area and to making it attractive even in very hot weather. They also contribute to noise abatement.

Unfortunately, the health and survival of the trees is being damaged by heavy foot and vehicle traffic through the tree pits. The tree pits also create tripping hazards and can be unsightly and muddy.

The Business Improvement Area wish to install decorative fences around the 119 tree pits, using Section 37 funds that were earmarked for greening the Yorkville area. This fencing would protect the trees and provide a unified aesthetic throughout the neighbourhood. The ABC Residents Association and the Greater Yorkville Residents Association support the request. Transportation Services has agreed to this request, in exchange for agreement by the Business Improvement Area to maintain the enclosures at its own expense.

The funding request is for $218,906 plus Harmonized Sales Tax.
2026.MM43.1.r:
Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks, recommends that:

1. City Council increase the 2026 Operating Budget for Non-Program on a one-time basis by $247,363 gross, $0 net, fully funded by Section 37 funds obtained from the development at 36, 38-48 Yorkville Avenue, 1263 Bay Street, 55 Scollard Street (Source Account: XR3026-3700290) secured for greening initiatives in the Yorkville area, to be used by the Bloor Yorkville Business Improvement Area to fabricate and install protective fencing for street trees in sidewalk pits on streets within the Bloor Yorkville Business Improvement Area boundaries, which may include Bellair Street, Cumberland Street, Yorkville Avenue, Hazelton Avenue, Scollard Street, and Bay Street (Cost Centre: NP2161).

2. City Council direct that the $247,363 be forwarded to the Bloor Yorkville Business Improvement Area upon the signing of an Undertaking to the satisfaction of the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, that governs the use of the funds and the financial reporting requirements and that the Business Improvement Area enters into a Memorandum of Understanding with the General Manager, Transportation Services that governs the Business Improvement Area’s maintenance obligations, including, but not limited to, design, installation, repair and upkeep, all at no cost to the City, and any other additional or amended conditions to the satisfaction of the General Manager, Transportation Services, in consultation with the Executive Director, Environment, Climate and Forestry, and in a form satisfactory to the City Solicitor.

2026.MM43.3.t: Heritage Designation Study - Sneaky Dee’s - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
2026.MM43.3.s:
Sneaky Dee’s is a historically and culturally significant music venue at 431 College Street. For generations, it has been a launching pad for local artists, a gathering place for friends and neighbours, and an important piece of Toronto's cultural identity. It is one of those places that gives our city its character.

On Friday, July 3, 2026, the applicant withdrew a redevelopment application (TE34.23) that would have demolished Sneaky Dee’s. This threat mobilized thousands of people across Toronto and beyond to Save Sneaky Dee’s. Residents organized. Musicians spoke out. Neighbours filled meetings, signed petitions, shared ideas, and refused to accept that one of Toronto's most beloved cultural institutions should disappear into yet another condo without exhausting every possible option. For everyone who has ever discovered a new band at Sneaky Dee’s, fallen in love, celebrated with friends over a plate of nachos, or simply believes Toronto should protect the places that make our city unique, this reprieve is worth celebrating.

This reprieve also gives the City a fresh opportunity to evaluate Sneaky Dee’s potential for a heritage designation. Dedicated volunteers have already begun to assemble supporting evidence.
2026.MM43.3.r:
Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, in consultation with the community, to evaluate the property at 431 College Street for designation under Part IV of the Ontario Heritage Act and to report back to the Toronto Preservation Board, to the Planning and Housing Committee and to Council in the first quarter of 2027.

2026.MM43.5.t: Activating Unused Seasonal Recreational Facilities in the Off-Season - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Amber Morley
2026.MM43.5.s:
Toronto’s recreational facilities are vital assets for our communities, providing space for residents to play, exercise and connect with their neighbours in a shared environment. As our City continues to grow, demand for access to recreational activities will grow as well. Securing new recreational space and ensuring we are getting the most out of existing space will be essential.

Some of Toronto’s recreational spaces are activated on a seasonal basis, such as ice pads, and may sit unused during the off-season. While there are examples of these spaces that are activated with alternative uses during the off-season in the City, this approach is not consistent. The City should adopt an approach that sees alternative programming, such as temporary pickleball courts or space for camps, deployed in our unused recreational space as a standard practice.

This approach would not only promote access to recreational opportunities for Torontonians – it could also support the City’s objectives for youth employment. Seasonal programming creates opportunities for short-term employment, ideal for students seeking work in the summer months.
2026.MM43.5.r:
Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Amber Morley, recommends that:

1. City Council request the General Manager, Parks and Recreation to explore options and report back in the first quarter of 2027 on opportunities to activate unused seasonal recreational space in City recreational facilities, such as inactive ice pads, during the off-season for uses including, but not limited to, pickleball and camps, and to consider opportunities to leverage any additional programming to support Toronto’s youth employment objectives.

2026.MM43.6.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for Capital Upgrades at Karma Co-op - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
2026.MM43.6.s:
Torontonians are expressing considerable concern about the rising cost of food. Toronto’s retail food supply is dominated by a small number of large grocery chains, but there are also some non-profit community food cooperatives. Co-ops maximize the affordability of quality food for members, while paying their staff a living wage, and building community through mutual aid, trading volunteer labour for reduced food costs, and eliminating commercial profit margins.

By 2026.MM.39.27, City Council requested the City Manager to report to the Economic and Community Development Committee in the second quarter of 2027 on options to support non-profit Toronto community food cooperatives, such as Karma Co-op. In the meantime, Karma Co-op has requested urgent Section 37 assistance to upgrade their garbage storage area. Karma Co-op is the only community food cooperative in Ward 11.

2026.MM43.7.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Toronto Chinatown Land Trust for a Mixed-Use Affordable Housing and Cultural Hub - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.7.s:
Councillor Saxe seeks authority to provide a non-profit community land trust, Toronto Chinatown Land Trust, with Section 37 funds in the amount of $700,000 to help purchase a mixed-use building in Ward 11 University-Rosedale, 81 Huron Street, to be operated as an anchor for the recently designated West Chinatown Cultural District.

Toronto Chinatown Land Trust is a community-supported non-profit devoted to preserving community space, affordable housing and commercial space in West Chinatown. The demand for culturally appropriate affordable housing in Chinatown far exceeds the supply. Worse, existing affordable housing and retail space is being lost. The Toronto Chinatown Land Trust and Canada Mortgage And Housing Corporation recently completed a research project documenting this urgency and the opportunity to preserve affordable housing that has been provided by family, clan, and regional associations.

The proposed building contains two commercial units on the ground floor and two residential units on the second floor that are currently used as illegal short-term rentals. If operated by Toronto Chinatown Land Trust in accordance with its proposed business plan, this building would be a first tangible step to address the residential and commercial displacement documented in Toronto Chinatown Land Trust’s research and in support of City Council’s designation of West Chinatown as a Cultural District.

The building would provide one unit of low-cost cultural space, one unit of commercial space for a culturally significant Chinatown business, and two units of affordable housing. The affordable housing would be operated under the terms of a municipal housing facility agreement with the Housing Secretariat comparable to the agreement used for recipients of Multi-Unit Residential Acquisition program funding. This motion also recommends municipal property tax relief for the two affordable homes for the 99-year term of affordability. A property tax exemption is a standard component of the Multi-Unit Residential Acquisition program.

The proposed cultural hub is inspired by Montreal’s Chinatown House, which hosts community exhibitions, lectures, workshops and socio-cultural events in leased space. The proposed Toronto Chinatown Land Trust space would be community-owned. Toronto Chinatown Land Trust has also undertaken to animate the Huron Plaza with culturally relevant activities and public art, both of which have been requested by the community. Economic Development and Culture advises that it has no funds available to support cultural space acquisition. However, they have reviewed the business plan and support Toronto Chinatown Land Trust’s request for these Section 37 funds.

To make this purchase possible and sustainable, Toronto Chinatown Land Trust is assembling private donations and a mortgage. The Section 37 funding proposed by this Motion is a key element to allow the purchase to proceed and will only be disbursed upon confirmation of Toronto Chinatown Land Trust’s purchase of the property and upon execution of appropriate agreements with the City, including conditions to safeguard the use of City funding and ensure that the property is maintained long-term as affordable housing and as a cultural and community hub. The proposed Section 37 funding must only be used for affordable housing and community space, and none of these funds may be used to subsidize the commercial unit.

2026.MM43.10.t: Addressing Moribund Development Sites - by Councillor Shelley Carroll, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.10.s:
The City of Toronto is experiencing a growing number of development sites where planning approvals have been granted, but construction has not proceeded due to broader economic conditions, financing challenges, and market uncertainty. While Council and other levels of government have taken steps to address barriers to housing construction and encourage the timely delivery of approved projects, the City also has a responsibility to ensure that properties within our communities are maintained to appropriate standards while they await redevelopment.

Across Toronto, residents and businesses are increasingly encountering properties that remain vacant, inactive, or in a prolonged state of transition. Regardless of the status of a future development application or approval, these properties continue to exist within established neighbourhoods and should be maintained in a manner that protects public safety, prevents deterioration, and supports the quality and appearance of surrounding communities. As the number of these sites has increased, so too has the impact on neighbourhoods across the city.

In October 2025, City Council adopted amendments through the Property Standards By-law: Phase II Review and Other Property Items to strengthen requirements for vacant properties and clarify owners’ obligations to protect properties from fire, accident, trespass, and other hazards. However, the current framework does not specifically address the unique circumstances of development sites that remain inactive for extended periods following planning approval.

A targeted review will examine whether the City’s existing property standards processes, service levels, enforcement tools, and interdivisional coordination are effectively addressing inactive and moribund development sites. The review will consider opportunities to improve training and guidance for enforcement staff, clarify jurisdiction and responsibilities across City divisions, identify available municipal remedies to ensure sites are maintained to appropriate standards, and explore options for improving site security and appearance while properties await construction.

Where additional legislative authority may be required, the review will also identify potential changes and engage with the Provincial Government to pursue any necessary amendments to ensure municipalities have appropriate tools to protect neighbourhoods and hold properties accountable.
2026.MM43.10.r:
Councillor Shelley Carroll, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, recommends that:

1. City Council request the City Manager, in consultation with the Executive Director, Municipal Licensing and Standards, and the Chief Building Official and Executive Director, Toronto Building, to report back to City Council in January 2027 on the effectiveness of the changes implemented through the Property Standards By-law: Phase II Review, including:

a. an assessment of whether the updated property standards framework is effectively addressing concerns related to vacant and inactive development sites, including sites where construction has not commenced following planning approval;

b. identification of any additional amendments, policies, or enforcement tools required to address development site-specific property standards concerns, including issues related to site maintenance, security, waste accumulation, fencing, landscaping, and other impacts on surrounding communities;

c. a review of training, guidance, and operational procedures provided to Municipal Licensing and Standards enforcement officers responsible for investigating property standards complaints involving vacant and inactive development sites, to ensure consistent application of existing standards and enforcement tools; and

d. an assessment of jurisdictional gaps or limitations that may prevent the City from effectively enforcing appropriate property standards on development sites, including a review of the legislative authorities available under the City of Toronto Act, 2006, and other applicable legislation.

2. City Council request the City Manager, in consultation with relevant City divisions, to explore opportunities to improve the appearance, safety, and security of inactive development sites awaiting construction, including options for enhanced site management requirements, improved fencing or screening standards, and other measures that can be implemented within the City’s existing authority.

3. City Council request the City Manager to include, as part of the report back, recommendations for any necessary by-law amendments, policy changes, operational improvements, or legislative advocacy required to ensure that inactive development sites are maintained to appropriate standards while respecting approved development permissions and the City’s objectives for housing and growth.

2026.MM43.11.t: Support for the Establishment of a National Fire Administration - by Councillor Paul Ainslie, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.11.s:
There are approximately 3,200 fire departments across Canada.

The scale and complexity of emergencies to which Canadian fire services are expected to respond have increased significantly in recent years and are expected to continue growing.

All governments have responsibilities related to fire protection, emergency management, disaster response, and public safety.

Effective collaboration and strategic coordination among governments and fire services are essential to ensure preparedness for major emergencies and the efficient deployment of resources.

The increasing frequency, severity, and duration of wildfires and other climate-related emergencies across Canada demonstrate the need for a coordinated and sustained national approach to prevention, mitigation, response, and recovery.

A National Fire Administration established within Public Safety Canada and developed in collaboration with Canada's fire chiefs and fire service organizations, would provide a coordinating mechanism for policy development, information sharing, research, training, and emergency management while respecting provincial and territorial jurisdiction.

Such an initiative would support communities in maintaining and replenishing critical emergency response equipment and ensuring local fire services remain adequately prepared to respond to emergencies.

A National Fire Administration would strengthen Canada's capacity to protect residents, businesses, critical infrastructure, and the economy while modernizing and enhancing the national emergency response framework.
2026.MM43.11.r:
Councillor Paul Ainslie, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, recommends that:

1. City Council express its support for the establishment of a National Fire Administration within Public Safety Canada, developed in collaboration with Canada's fire chiefs and fire service organizations.

2. City Council forward a copy of this motion to the Federal Minister of Public Safety Canada, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, Toronto's Members of Parliament, and Ontario's Minister of the Solicitor General.

2026.MM43.13.t: 743 Warden Avenue - Amending Section 37 Agreement for Blocks 6, 7 and 8 Plan 66M-2549 - by Councillor Paul Ainslie, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
2026.MM43.13.s:
In 2013, Official Plan Amendment, Zoning By-law Amendment, Draft Plan of Subdivision and Site Plan Control applications were submitted for the lands at 743 Warden Avenue. The applications sought permission for 202 residential townhouse units, three commercial buildings, a network of public roads and lanes, a public park, and a storm water management pond.

Following appeal by the applicant and a subsequent settlement hearing endorsed by City Council in 2015 (Item 2015.CC8.2), the former Ontario Municipal Board approved, in principle, the draft Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment and Draft Plan of Subdivision to re-designate the lands from Employment Areas to Mixed Use Areas and Neighbourhoods as per the recommended settlement.

The site specific zoning by-law (By-law 528-2016 (OMB)) established three primary phases of development: Phase 1 (Blocks 1-5 and 9-20); Phase 2 (Block 21 and/or Block 22); Phase 3 (Blocks 6, 7 and 8); and Phase 4 (the remaining Block 21 or Block 22 if only one of these blocks is constructed as part of Phase 2). Blocks 6, 7 and 8 were identified as Phase 3 in part to ensure co-ordination of certain required municipal road infrastructure for those lands and in part to ensure co-ordination of the commercial and residential blocks within the development, particularly commercial Blocks 21 and 22. Along with the addition of a holding provision in the By-law for Blocks 6, 7 and 8, the sequencing of all of the phases were to be further set out.

A Section 37 Agreement, dated December 7, 2015, was registered on title for the lands at 743 Warden Avenue (AT4254031) (the "Section 37 Agreement"). In addition to securing community benefits, the Section 37 Agreement secured the phasing set out in the zoning amendment as a legal convenience. Specifically, Sections 4.6 and 4.7 included provisions for sequencing construction and linked building permits and completion of construction on at least one of Block 21 and 22 prior to construction on Blocks 6, 7 and 8.

The final Plan of Subdivision was registered on June 25, 2018 as 66M-2549. The associated Subdivision Agreement, dated March 28, 2017, was registered on title (AT4908517) and also included phasing provisions.

The original objective of the phasing had been to build in an incentive to build out the commercial blocks coincidental to the larger residential component Phase 1 of the development, which is now complete.

In 2023 the owner requested adjustment of the construction phasing language in the Section 37 Agreement to allow for construction of residential Blocks 6 to 8 (Phase 3) to proceed concurrently with, not subsequent to, commercial Blocks 21 and 22 (Phase 2/4) on certain conditions. At its meeting on February 6 and 7, 2024, City Council adopted Item 2024.SC 10.6 and approved amendment to the Section 37 Agreement to adjust the construction of phasing provisions and allow for concurrent construction provided that building permits had been issued and construction commenced relating to the commercial blocks. An amending Section 37 Agreement, dated April 23, 2024, was executed and registered (AT6574560). A corresponding amending Subdivision Agreement, dated April 23, 2024, was also approved and executed by the Director of Community Planning and subsequently registered (AT6574562).

The holding provisions relating to the residential Blocks 6, 7 and 8 were lifted by By-law 189-2024(PLN) enacted March 15, 2024. At its meeting on December 16 and 17, 2025, City Council assumed the roads and services within the Subdivision (Item 2025.SC 27.3) and subsequently enacted assumption By-law 345-2026.

A request has now been made by the applicant to further amend the Section 37 Agreement to allow development of the remaining residential Blocks 6, 7 and 8 to proceed following the provision of Notice of Approval Conditions for site plan approval for either commercial Block 21 or 22. The Director, Community Planning, Scarborough District is supportive of a similar further revision to the Subdivision Agreement, as amended. This will enable completion of the residential component of the subdivision and allow the construction of much needed housing on Blocks 6, 7 and 8 to proceed expeditiously and still allow either or both of Block 21 and Block 22 to proceed to development concurrently.
2026.MM43.13.r:
Councillor Paul Ainslie, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks, recommends that:

City Council authorize the City Solicitor, in consultation with the Executive Director, Development Review, to amend the Section 37 Agreement, dated December 7, 2015 (AT4254031), between Zahavish Downtown Developments Ltd. and the City of Toronto, entered into pursuant to Section 37 of the Planning Act (as it read the day before the date Section 1 of Schedule 17 of the COVID-19 Economic Recovery Act, 2020, came into force), as amended by an Amending Agreement, dated April 23, 2024 (AT6574560), to further adjust construction phasing provisions allowing for concurrent construction of the final phase of the residential blocks (Blocks 6, 7 and 8 66M-2549) and commercial blocks (Blocks 21 and 22 66M-2549) on terms further set out in the amending agreement, including that Notice of Site Plan Approval Conditions will have been issued in connection with one or both of the commercial blocks.

2. City Council authorize City Officials to take such action as necessary to implement the recommendation above, including execution and registration of necessary agreement(s).

2026.MM43.14.t: Securing A Permanent Facility for the Central Eglinton Community Centre - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
2026.MM43.14.s:
The Central Eglinton Community Centre, located at 160 Eglinton Avenue East, is an integral part of the Yonge-Eglinton community, providing a wide range of services focused on the needs of seniors, families, and newcomers. Central Eglinton Community Centre operates approximately 16,000 square feet of space to serve a growing community.

Central Eglinton Community Centre is one of ten community centres known as the Association of Community Centres. Each is managed by a volunteer Board of Management appointed by City Council, and the group receives its funding through the annual Council-approved Operating Budget. These multi-purpose facilities provide inclusive spaces that strengthen civic engagement, build local leadership, and advance equity-focused outcomes. The City Council-adopted Association of Community Centres Expansion Framework and Implementation Strategy affirm the Association of Community Centres model as essential community development infrastructure that advances neighbourhood resilience.

The AOCC portfolio faces significant state of good repair obligations, as well as expansion and relocation pressures. The Council-directed Association of Community Centres Facilities and Operations Plan (2025.EC24.2) will build on the Implementation Strategy by establishing a prioritized, citywide, multi-year framework to support the long-term sustainability and strategic growth of the Association of Community Centres portfolio. Through this Plan, Social Development and Corporate Real Estate Management will assess facility renewal and capital improvement needs across all Association of Community Centres locations.

Unlike most Association of Community Centres, Central Eglinton Community Centre is one of only two centres that operate out of privately owned space rather than a City facility. The City leases the space at 160 Eglinton Avenue East on the Centre's behalf. That tenure is now at risk. On November 14, 2024, City Council approved an Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment application (2024.TE17.6) for the redevelopment of 150 to 164 Eglinton Avenue East and 134 and 140 Redpath Avenue. The approval permits a two-tower, 61-storey mixed-use development. The existing buildings on the site, including the building housing Central Eglinton Community Centre's facility, will be demolished to accommodate the new development. Planning approvals are now in place, and the landowner is advancing redevelopment plans; Central Eglinton Community Centre is expected to face displacement pressure in the near term, necessitating the identification and securing of a permanent replacement location.

City staff and the local Councillor's office have worked to identify various relocation opportunities in the Yonge-Eglinton area, including community space in new developments and potential City acquisitions. No long-term solution has been secured to date. This motion directs City staff to continue and intensify that work, so that Central Eglinton Community Centre has a permanent home in the community before its current lease expires. Should the City pursue acquisitions, future capital budget requests will be required. This motion requests that staff make the appropriate requests through future budgets to ensure acquisition plans are adequately resourced.
2026.MM43.14.r:
Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management, the Executive Director, Social Development, in consultation with the Chief Executive Officer, CreateTO, to continue pursuing options to secure a long-term space for the Central Eglinton Community Centre within their catchment area, including space secured through new developments and potential property acquisitions.

2. City Council direct the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management and the Executive Director, Social Development, to identify and recommend a long-term facility solution for the Central Eglinton Community Centre through the Association of Community Centres Facilities and Operations Plan, including any funding or budget implications for consideration through the City's Budget process, and to report back to the Economic and Community Development Committee as part of the Facilities and Operations Plan in the first quarter of 2028.

2026.MM43.15.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for the Creation and Installation of a Plaque to Commemorate Research Enterprises Limited - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
2026.MM43.15.s:
This Motion seeks authorization to release $10,000 in Section 37 (Planning Act Reserve Account) funds to Heritage Toronto for the creation and installation of a plaque to commemorate Research Enterprises Limited.

Research Enterprises Limited was a short-lived Toronto-based Crown Corporation that built electronics and optical instruments during the Second World War. During this time, they became Leaside's largest employer.

At its peak, the company's plants covered most of the area between Eglinton Avenue, Laird Drive, and Research Road, along with smaller shops and storage extending to Wicksteed Avenue further south. In total, the company estate covered 22 hectares, had 70,000 square metres of floor space, employed 7,500 men and women, and produced $220 million worth of radar systems and optical instruments that helped the Allies win the war.

After Research Enterprises Limited was closed, their factories formed the basis of a Corning Glass plant, Philips Electronics, and a variety of other firms. Today only a few of the original buildings still stand, used primarily for light industrial and small commercial enterprises.

This Heritage Toronto plaque will mark the history of Research Enterprises Limited and the Canadian war effort in Leaside and will compliment planned interpretive signs in Radar Park.

Utility infrastructure located within the public right-of-way is essential to ensuring residents have access to telephone, internet, and cable services. However, utility wires are frequently left open to easy inadvertent damage when buried to an insufficient depth, draped over fences, or left on top of grass.

Improperly installed utility cables and infrastructure are easily damaged and these incidents can result in prolonged service outages, leaving residents without access to vital communications and internet connectivity for multiple days. Utility providers should be accountable for service interruptions and provide customers with appropriate bill reductions or refunds when outages occur due to shoddy work.

2026.MM43.21.t: Enhancing Tenant Safety Through a Review of Toronto Community Housing Corporation CCTV Camera Coverage, Visitor Verification Measures and Related Policies - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
2026.MM43.21.s:
Tenant safety remains one of the most frequently raised concerns in Toronto Community Housing Corporation communities across the City of Toronto.

Recent community safety meetings hosted by my office and Toronto Community Housing Corporation at Moss Park Apartments and at the Wellesley Community Centre for St. James Town residents brought together tenants, Toronto Community Housing Corporation staff, Toronto Police Service, the City's Violence Intervention and Support Unit, Fred Victor, and Unison Health and Community Services to discuss local safety concerns and identify solutions.

Tenants consistently raised concerns regarding building security, unauthorized entry, trespassing, anti-social behaviour, access control, package theft, and recurring safety issues within residential buildings. Many tenants also expressed concern about their ability to identify individuals at their door before opening it, particularly seniors, families with children, newcomers, persons living alone, and other vulnerable residents.

As a result of these discussions, Toronto Community Housing Corporation has undertaken Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design reviews and committed to reviewing camera coverage and access control measures in affected communities. While these efforts are welcome, a broader review is warranted to identify opportunities to strengthen building security and enhance tenant safety across Toronto Community Housing Corporation communities.

CCTV cameras can be a critical tool in responding to safety incidents and, while they should not be viewed as a stand-alone solution, they are an important component of a broader community safety framework. At the same time, many tenants indicated that the ability to safely verify who is at their door or seeking access to their building would improve their sense of security and comfort within their homes.

Tenants also raised concerns regarding their ability to verify the identity of individuals seeking access to their building through existing intercom and buzzer systems. In some communities, tenants expressed interest in technologies or security devices that would allow them to visually confirm the identity of visitors before granting access to a residential building or opening their door.

Where documented safety concerns exist and access control or visitor verification measures may be limited, absent, or insufficient, tenants have expressed interest in additional security measures, including tenant-operated peephole cameras, door-view cameras, and other non-invasive security devices that may assist residents in identifying visitors and enhancing personal safety.

In some communities, tenants have already installed or expressed interest in installing non-invasive security devices to support personal safety and visitor verification. Many tenants indicated that these devices are being considered or installed for safety purposes and to assist with identifying visitors before granting access to their home or residential building.

A review of Toronto Community Housing Corporation's current policies respecting CCTV camera coverage, tenant-installed security devices, visitor verification measures, and related building access systems could help identify further opportunities to support tenant safety while ensuring alignment with applicable legal, privacy, building, fire/life safety, operational, and financial considerations.

2026.MM43.23.t: Authority to Accept Donations from Midtown Ravines Group for the Vale of Avoca Improvement Project - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
2026.MM43.23.s:
The City of Toronto and Toronto and Region Conservation Authority have initiated the Vale of Avoca Improvement Project, in the Yellow Creek ravine near Yonge Street and St. Clair Ave East. This project will develop a coordinated plan to mitigate erosion hazards, enhance natural features, and improve how people access, move through and experience the Vale of Avoca ravine. The ravine straddles Toronto wards University-Rosedale and Toronto-St. Paul’s.

The erosion hazards present risks to municipal infrastructure, trails, access points to the ravine, and adjacent properties. Certain informal trails are in poor condition, and two staircases providing access to the ravine have been closed. Without the construction of adequate erosion control measures, the banks will continue to erode, and slope instabilities will worsen.

The proposed scope of work for this project includes site evaluation, engagement and design services to develop a coordinated ravine improvement plan that:

- stabilizes the creek, protects the long-term stable top of bank, and mitigates erosion hazards;

- preserves and enhances natural features; and

- improves how people access, move through and experience the ravine system.

In 2026, Toronto and Region Conservation Authority released an request for proposal to procure a proponent to carry out these professional services.

The Midtown Ravine Group is a registered charity created by ten local residents’ associations, formed to raise consciousness about the state of midtown ravines, raise funds for improvements, and mobilize community participation in ravine stewardship. Midtown Ravine Group is actively participating in stakeholder engagement with the City and Toronto and Region Conservation Authority.

Midtown Ravine Group wishes to fundraise and contribute funds to the Vale of Avoca Improvement Project. Donations would be put towards projects approved by the City and Toronto and Region Conservation Authority project team, in consultation with Midtown Ravine Group, with a focus on amenities that improve trail user experience in the ravine. Midtown Ravine Group also wishes to donate in-kind services to the project related to Invasive Species Mapping, an Ecological Land Classification Report, and a Baseline Biological Inventories Report.

The recommendations in this Motion would provide the necessary authority for the City to accept and spend the donated funds. While the final amount Midtown Ravine Group will be able to fundraise is unknown, it is expected to be more than $50,000. Under the City of Toronto Donation Policy, any donation from one donor exceeding $50,000 per year requires City Council authority to accept.

This motion is urgent to allow fundraising and agreement planning to proceed in alignment with the projected Vale of Avoca Improvement Project schedule.

2026.MM43.25.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for Clock Tower Trail Wayfinding and Placemaking Pole Wraps - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe
2026.MM43.25.s:
The Clock Tower Trail is a pedestrian walking route along existing sidewalks and laneways in downtown Toronto. This loop through the Bay Cloverhill and Church Wellesley neighbourhoods connects residents to existing and new parks, public spaces, and public art. Teams from City Planning, Parks and Recreation, and Transportation Services have worked with the members of Bay Cloverhill Community Association to determine this route.

"The Clock Tower Trail" name is inspired by the historic St. Charles Clock Tower at 484 to 488 Yonge Street. This loop extends north and south on both sides of Yonge Street between Charles Street East and McGill Street. On the east side, the trail runs south from George Hislop Park to Joseph Sheard Parkette, while on the west side, the trail runs north from College Park, turning north through Dr. Lilliam McGregor Park, Clover Hill Park and St. Mary Street Parkette.

This motion seeks City Council authorization to release and allocate Section 37 funds to Transportation Services, for the procurement and installation of pole wraps on existing hydro poles and traffic signal poles within the right-of-way along the route of the Clock Tower Trail. The new pole wraps will provide wayfinding graphics that provide visual cues along the Clock Tower Trail, creating a cohesive experience for residents and visitors.

As Regent Park continues to grow and evolve, the delivery of permanent community infrastructure is critical to building a complete community where residents have access to the spaces, services, and opportunities needed to participate fully in neighbourhood life.

Association of Community Centres are community-governed, multi-purpose facilities overseen by volunteer Boards of Management appointed by City Council. These facilities provide affordable space for residents, grassroots groups, community organizations, and local initiatives, while advancing community development and resident leadership. The Council-adopted Association of Community Centre Expansion Framework and Implementation Strategy affirm the Association of Community Centre model as essential community development infrastructure that advances neighbourhood resilience.

As part of City Council's approval of Regent Park Phases 4 and 5, community space and a new Toronto Public Library branch were secured through the redevelopment. During detailed planning discussions, an opportunity was identified to expand the future library site to accommodate a new Association of Community Centre facility, co-located with the future Parliament Street District Library Branch. Located within Regent Park's future civic square, this facility would serve as a permanent community hub and civic anchor for local residents and the broader Downtown East.

This motion authorizes the release of Section 37 funds to facilitate the design, construction and full fit-out of a new community space that will be co-located with the future Toronto Public Library Parliament Street District Branch, creating an integrated civic hub and enabling the establishment of a new Association of Community Centre facility in Regent Park.

2026.MM43.27.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Support Indigenous Placekeeping in Allan Gardens - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
2026.MM43.27.s:
This Motion seeks authorization to release Section 37 community benefits funds, in the amount of $350,000, to support Indigenous placekeeping capital improvements in Allan Gardens. A portion of this funding will be allocated to the Friends of Allan Gardens to support engagement with relevant Indigenous communities and organizations in collaboration with City staff and relevant partners. These groups will be actively engaged in co-stewardship and the co-development of a long-term vision and will select a community-identified name for the project, replacing the placeholder name included in this motion.

Allan Gardens is a historical and contemporary gathering place for many Indigenous peoples and organizations. This significance is noted in the Toronto City Council-endorsed “Growing with the City: An Ecosystem of Initiatives in Allan Gardens”. Since 2022, a Sacred Fire has been burning in Allan Gardens as a living site of mourning, healing, and ceremony, maintained by Fire Keepers — Indigenous community members who tend a Fire of Mourning in recognition of each child whose remains have been recovered from the grounds of former residential schools across Canada.

Friends of Allan Gardens has an established role in park stewardship and community programming at Allan Gardens. This Motion provides a clearer path for Friends of Allan Gardens to support inclusive engagement on the future of Indigenous placekeeping in Allan Gardens, while ensuring the City retains appropriate oversight for funding, agreements, capital improvements, and reporting back to Council.

The proposed funding will support engagement and planning in a manner that recognizes Indigenous self-determination, and the City’s commitments under the Reconciliation Action Plan. The intent is to ensure that future site improvements are informed by community input, operational feasibility, and clear City accountability.

2026.MM43.30.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for a Heritage Plaque for CHUM Radio - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe
2026.MM43.30.s:
In Toronto, teens and their hip parents all listened to CHUM radio. Interspersed with its influential Top Fifty music chart were outrageous promotions, contests, and the larger-than-life personalities of its DJs.

The station was original, audacious, and irreverent. Amid CHUM’s hipness were serious broadcasters like Harvey Kirck, who later became the national news anchor at CTV; Monty Hall, who rose to fame as host of the U.S. program Let’s Make a Deal; Larry Mann, who became a Hollywood actor; and Jeanne Becker, who went on to MuchMusic and Fashion Television. Both CHUM-AM and CHUM-FM made a huge impact on Toronto.

CHUM-AM switched to a rock ‘n’ roll format on May 27, 1957. Elvis Presley’s “All Shook Up” was the first song played. CHUM pioneered rock broadcasting in Toronto, hosting many noteworthy concerts including, among others, visits to Maple Leaf Gardens by Elvis Presley (1957) and the Beatles (1964, 1965, and 1966). CHUM-FM switched to rock in 1968. Rick Moranis was one if its popular DJs.

Any musician of note passing through Toronto—from Elvis and Buddy Holly to Paul Anka and Gordon Lightfoot—made sure that a stopover at CHUM was part of the itinerary. CHUM is recognized by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a significant station in music history.

CHUM was based at 1331 Yonge Street. The plaque will be installed near the intersection of Yonge Street and Jackes Avenue.

This motion seeks authorization to amend the 2026 Operating Budget of Heritage Toronto to fund the creation and installation of a plaque commemorating the history of CHUM radio in Toronto. Heritage Toronto had estimated the entire project to cost $10,000.

2026.MM43.34.s:
Over the next 30 years Downsview will be re-developed with an estimated 115,000 new residents and 52,000 new jobs across 15 new neighbourhoods. 2026.MM43.35.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds Gardiner Gateways East Project - Intersection and Underpass Improvements at Lower Jarvis, Lower Sherbourne, Lower Parliament and Cherry Streets - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
2026.MM43.35.s:
The Under Gardiner Public Realm Plan was developed as a collaboration between the City and The Bentway and was approved by Toronto City Council in April 2024 (https://secure.toronto.ca/council/agenda-item.do?item=2024.IE12.5). The plan sets out a long-term vision for the 7km elevated Gardiner corridor, establishing new standards for safety, identity, amenity and ecology, and informing future planning of the public realm from Dufferin Street to the Don Valley Parkway.

The City is continuing its partnership with The Bentway to implement the Under Gardiner Public Realm Plan by working with BIAs, institutions, and businesses and landowners to advance the Under Gardiner Public Realm Plan, including the goal of removing barriers and making new connections along the elevated Gardiner corridor through public realm improvement projects. One of the strategies is to improve the ‘north - south’ experience of crossing through the underpass intersections using pedestrian lighting, enhanced wayfinding and additional placemaking features.

The Waterfront Business Improvement Area’s Strategic Framework (2017) and ‘Waterfront Reconnect’ (2019) vision document, highlights the goal of improving ‘north - south’ connectivity through public realm improvements and ultimately achieving success in boosting business growth in the area.

The Old Town Business Improvement Area’s 2024 Streetscape Transformation Strategy emphasizes the benefits of enhancing and accessibility for all ROW users and optimizing corridor operations through an incremental approach.

Building upon the success of recent intersection improvements at Dan Leckie Way/Lake Shore Boulevard West (2025) and Bathurst Street/Lake Shore Boulevard West (2026), this motion secures agreements and funding for Gardiner intersection improvements and rail corridor improvements at four locations, Lower Jarvis, Lower Sherbourne, Lower Parliament and Cherry streets (“Gardiner Gateways East Project”). This Gardiner Gateways East Project proposes to integrate improvements of both the under-Gardiner spaces and the Union Station Rail Corridor underpasses (teamways’). These teamway spaces act as an additional barrier to the waterfront beyond the Gardiner Expressway, and suffer from inadequate lighting, poor visibility, poor wayfinding and unfavourable conditions for pedestrians making their way to waterfront. The revitalization of these underpasses through improved lighting and wayfinding will increase North South connectivity in line with the goals of the Under-Gardiner Public Realm Plan and the public realm frameworks.

To achieve this goal, the City’s Business Improvement Area Office, through its Capital Cost Share Streetscape Improvement Program, will collaborate with The Waterfront Business Improvement Area and Old Town Business Improvement Area, to engage The Bentway to pursue this Gardiner Gateways East Project for the intersections and underpasses located at Lower Jarvis and Lower Sherbourne streets. The Bentway would oversee design and construction of pedestrian lighting, on behalf of the City and the Business Improvement Areas, to be funded by the City’s Capital Cost Share Program.

The City, through the City Planning Division, will further support this Gardiner Gateways East Project to include the four intersections and underpasses located at Lower Jarvis, Lower Sherbourne, Lower Parliament and Cherry, and proposes additional funding through Section 37 as recommended.

Based on past project precedents including Rees Street (2019), Simcoe Street (2023), York Street (2023), Dan Leckie Way (2025) and Bathurst Street (2026), the City’s Business Improvement Area Office and City Planning support this initiative and integral role of The Bentway towards facilitating and managing this Gardiner Gateways East Project from design through to construction.

2026.MM43.37.t: Supporting Continued Investments in the Toronto Harbour Nautical Centre at Harbourfront Centre - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Amber Morley
2026.MM43.37.s:
The Toronto Harbour Nautical Centre, formerly Harbourfront Centre Sailing and Powerboating, provides sailing, powerboating, paddling, boat-rental and related marine programming on Toronto’s central waterfront. The facility is currently operated by York Bay Marine Services Inc., including the delivery of water-based programming for Harbourfront Centre’s children’s camp.

York Bay Marine Services Inc. and Harbourfront Centre have agreed in principle to a 25-year operating arrangement for the facility. The operator has advised that a longer-term agreement is needed to support continued investment in the Nautical Centre, including improvements to its fleet, docks, systems, building and surrounding grounds. The operator has stated that it has already invested approximately $450,000 but has been unable to secure financing for further capital and leasehold improvements while operating under a shorter-term arrangement.

The City owns the lands and leases them to Harbourfront Centre under a long-term lease dated December 9, 1997. That lease permits Harbourfront Centre to enter into subleases and licences of up to five years with the City’s consent but does not currently permit a sublease or licences for a longer term.

2026.MM43.38.t: Seeing the Forest and the Trees: Preserving the Green Space, Ravines, Structures and Tree Canopy with Public Accessibility, Security and Maintenance at the Forest Valley Outdoor Centre - by Councillor James Pasternak, seconded by Councillor Jamaal Myers
2026.MM43.38.s:
Forest Valley Outdoor Centre is located on Toronto and Region Conservation Authority lands in York Centre (Ward 6) and is managed by the City of Toronto. The site has a rich history in which thousands of past and present Torontonians have enjoyed the river, ravines, green space and forests either when it was a privately owned day camp or as a City of Toronto asset.

Until recently, the lands were leased seasonally to the Toronto District School Board. At one time, the City of Toronto operated summer day camps on the site. The site also has a wide range of structures and meeting places, which have been used in the past for permitted events. The terms of the ending of the lease agreement with the Toronto District School Board are evolving. Should the agreement be terminated, it is likely the City will continue to manage the lands and associated buildings/assets on behalf of Toronto and Region Conservation Authority.

In light of these changes in use, a new strategic plan is needed to ensure Forest Valley Outdoor Centre remains well-maintained, safe, active, and in a state of good repair under a renewed agreement with the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority. The updated plan should preserve the site's valuable green space, ravines, and tree canopy while ensuring continued public access, effective maintenance, and long-term sustainability.

2026.MM43.40.t: Advancing a Heritage Conservation District for Corktown - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik
2026.MM43.40.s:
This motion is to request staff review the Corktown neighbourhood for its potential to become a future heritage conservation district (HCD).

The neighbourhood, largely bounded between Shuter Street to the north, Front Street/Eastern Avenue to the south, Berkeley Street to the west and the Don River to the east, has a number of listed heritage properties that were identified through the 2019 update to the King Parliament Secondary Plan.

From that report:

The King-Parliament area includes some of Toronto’s oldest neighbourhoods and commercial and industrial areas. Within its boundaries are cultural heritage resources, including built heritage, cultural heritage landscapes, and archaeology that reflect the long evolution of the area, from ancient Indigenous habitation through the late-18th century founding of the Town of York, to the present day. The contemporary road network and built form of the area reflects its evolution from a primarily residential and commercial area in the first half of the 19th century, to a commercial and industrial area with pockets of working class housing by the end of the 20th century.

Following a canvas of Corktown residents, a local resident and heritage advocate, Coralina Lemos, reached out to my office requesting support to move a potential HCD for her neighbourhood forward.

With this background and neighbourhood support, I believe it is therefore appropriate to evaluate the Corktown neighbourhood for its potential for a future HCD study in earnest.

2026.MM43.42.t: Pedestrian Safety Improvements Surrounding Yonge Street and Eglinton Avenue - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
2026.MM43.42.s:
With an average of 4,500 pedestrians per hour, Yonge Street and Eglinton Avenue is one of the busiest pedestrian intersections in Toronto. As the local community is keenly aware, pedestrian congestion extends well beyond the intersection and into the surrounding neighborhood. With the long-awaited opening of the Eglinton Crosstown LRT, it is time to reimagine the Yonge and Eglinton corridor to better serve the tens of thousands of pedestrians who navigate the crossings every day.

This motion recommends the installation of a pedestrian priority phase, also known as a “pedestrian scramble,” at two intersections: Yonge Street and Eglinton Avenue, and Roehampton Avenue and Orchard View Boulevard.

At both intersections, a pedestrian scramble would minimize pedestrian delay, accommodate the significant crossing demand associated with the Toronto Transit Commission and LRT stations, reduce pedestrian-vehicle conflicts and improve the overall pedestrian experience in the neighborhood. Coordinating the introduction of these scrambles with signal retiming at neighboring intersections ensures that improved pedestrian safety and convenience can be achieved while mitigating congestion concerns.

Pedestrian safety concerns along Roehampton Avenue and Broadway Avenue are also addressed in this motion. In 2021, one-way designations were introduced along both streets to support significant construction activity in the area. This motion proposes additional signage to support the current functioning of the roadways and outlines a plan to comprehensively review the one-way designations once construction diminishes.

This motion represents a rare win-win: an opportunity to improve pedestrian safety and convenience at two of Toronto’s busiest pedestrian intersections without sacrificing commuter travel times. As the Yonge-Eglinton neighborhood continues to grow, I ask Council to support my motion to bring much needed pedestrian safety improvements to the Yonge Street and Eglinton Avenue area.

2. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services to evaluate the implementation of an exclusive pedestrian phase at Yonge Street and Roehampton Avenue/Orchard View Boulevard to be implemented in 2027 as part of the same initiative, subject to consideration through the 2027 budget process and Council approval of the funding and resource requirements, taking into account other City priorities.

3. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services to undertake coordinated signal timing optimization for the Yonge Street corridor between Soudan Avenue/Berwick Avenue and Montgomery Avenue/Broadway Avenue to minimize impacts on traffic operations, subject to consideration through the 2027 budget process and Council approval of the funding and resource requirements, taking into account other City priorities.

4. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services to report back to City Council in 2030 with recommendations on the feasibility of returning Broadway Avenue and Roehampton Avenue to two-way operations.

5. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services to install additional signage and pavement markings along Broadway Avenue and Roehampton Avenue to improve the temporary one-way operation of both streets and enhance pedestrian, subject to consideration through the 2027 budget process and Council approval of the funding and resource requirements, taking into account other City priorities.

6. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services to monitor the operation of the Pedestrian Priority Phases introduced through this initiative, and report back in the first quarter of 2028 on their effectiveness.

2026.MM43.44.t: Increase Resources for Tree Maintenance and Arborist Staffing - by Councillor Nick Mantas, seconded by Councillor Paul Ainslie
2026.MM43.44.s:
The City of Toronto's urban forest is one of the largest municipally managed urban forests in North America and plays a critical role in improving air quality, reducing urban heat, managing stormwater, enhancing biodiversity, and improving the overall quality of life for residents. There is a commitment to increase Toronto's tree canopy to 40 percent by 2050, resulting in a growing inventory of trees that require ongoing maintenance; and

Many neighbourhoods across the City are experiencing significant delays in routine tree pruning, resulting in safety concerns, obstructed sidewalks and roadways, reduced visibility, and increased service requests from residents. Proper and timely tree pruning is essential to maintaining the health of Toronto's urban forest, protecting public safety, and reducing the risk of damage caused by dead or hazardous branches.
2026.MM43.44.r:
Councillor Nick Mantas, seconded by Councillor Paul Ainslie, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the Executive Director, Environment Climate and Forestry, in consultation with the appropriate City divisions, to report back in the first quarter of 2027 with an assessment on increasing staffing levels for tree maintenance and pruning and include the budget impacts, such report to include:

a. the current backlog for routine tree pruning and maintenance across all districts;

b. the estimated number of additional arborists and forestry staff required to reduce service delays and maintain a sustainable pruning cycle;

c. the financial implications of increasing staffing levels; and

d. options to accelerate proactive tree maintenance as Toronto's tree canopy continues to expand.

2. City Council request the Mayor to consider allocating additional funding through the 2027 Budget process to support the hiring of additional arborists and forestry staff to ensure the City's growing urban forest is maintained safely, efficiently, and proactively.

2026.MM43.45.t: Re-opening and Amending Item 2026.EX31.8 - Amendments to the Toronto Transit Commission Records Retention Schedule (Municipal Code Chapter 219, Records, Corporate (Local Boards)) - by Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Paul Ainslie
2026.MM43.45.s:
At its meeting on May 20, 2026, City Council, adopted upon consent, Item 2026.EX31.8. This decision purported to amend Chapter 219, Records, Corporate (Local Boards) in a specific manner.

The method in which the Toronto Transit Commission communicated the proposed amendments to Chapter 219, Records, Corporate (Local Boards) to the City rendered the proposal ineffective.

The City’s Municipal Code, establishes a Corporate Records Retention Committee, which is required to review proposed amendments to record retention provisions prior to consideration by City Council. The Corporate Records Retention Committee task is to ensure that such proposals meet the relevant legal and operational requirements to be validly implemented, if approved by Council. For this reason, City’s Municipal Code expressly indicates that no record retention schedule may be reviewed, established or amended, by Council unless the prior approval of the Corporate Records Retention Committee has been obtained. This is to ensure that Council only considers proposed amendments to various retention obligations, which are capable of being implemented.

The proposed amendments to Chapter 219, were not presented to Corporate Records Retention Committee prior to decision of the Toronto Transit Commission as articulated at its Meeting No. 14, as item TTC.14.13, prior to being communicated to City Council. The proposed amendment was procedurally prohibited from being effective, as it contravened the requirements of the City’s Municipal Code for such decisions. This means that the proposed updates can not be implemented.

The proposed updated Records Retention Schedule, would implement several useful modifications to strengthen Toronto Transit Commission’s information governance framework while enhancing the clarity, usability, and operational relevance of the record retention requirements applicable to the Toronto Transit Commission. These modifications include: Disposition Adjustments: Revised retention periods for 41 record series to ensure alignment with current business workflows, risk considerations, and legislative obligations; Consolidation/removal of Existing Record Series and addition of New Record Series: 13 record series have been consolidated or removed while Two new record series have been added to address emerging business requirements and new types of documentation generated through Toronto Transit Commission operations.; as well as Administrative and Clarity Improvements: 138 record series, were modified by correcting inconsistencies, and enhancing clarity of the wording as to support more efficient application.

The proposed amendments in Item 2026.EX21.8 were not in an appropriate format aligned with record retention standards. The Corporate Records Retention Committee has reviewed the proposed amendments, and ensured the proposed amendments are now presented in a format that meets the relevant requirements, and has issued an approval thereof. A copy of this approval is available in Attachment 1.

This matter is urgent because City Council authority is required to allow for the Toronto Transit Commission to commence to manage its records in accordance with the proposed retention schedule.

City Council Item 2026.EX31.8 (May 20 and 21, 2026).

2026.MM43.46.t: Modernizing the City’s Permit Parking Program and Managing On-Street Parking Demand in Toronto's Growing Neighbourhoods - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
2026.MM43.46.s:
In many neighbourhoods within Davenport, residents have expressed concerns about the growing competition for available on-street parking spaces.

Multuplix permissions have encouraged gentle density in established neighbourhoods. While multi-unit residences provide more housing options and expand supply, they may also generate additional demand for on-street parking.

In addition, under the City’s current on-street permit parking program, households are able to obtain permits for multiple vehicles at a single address, with no limit on the number of permits that can be issued. This can reduce availability for other residents and create challenges for visitors, service providers, and neighbouring households.

Reviewing permit eligibility and establishing reasonable limits could help ensure more fairness with available parking, while also supporting the City’s broader strategies related to the management of the parking supply and the use of more sustainable modes of transportation as our city grows. Permit limits may encourage reduced reliance on private vehicles while preserving parking availability for residents who rely on on-street parking. A review would allow the City to determine whether current permit policies remain appropriate in the context of increasing density and evolving transportation patterns.
2026.MM43.46.r:
Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks, recommends that:

1. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services, as part of the Residential Parking Review currently underway, to review the City's residential on-street permit parking program to:

a. assess the eligibility criteria for residential on-street parking permits in areas experiencing increased residential density, including neighbourhoods with multiplex and other multi-unit housing developments; and

b. evaluate options for establishing reasonable limits on the number of residential on-street parking permits that may be issued to a single property or household, taking into consideration neighbourhood parking demand, equity of access to on-street parking, and the availability of off-street parking.

2026.MM43.47.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Support Community Stewardship Improvements at the Rosewood Pollinator Community Garden - by Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
2026.MM43.47.s:
The Rosewood Pollinator Community Garden is a community stewardship initiative operated by the Scarborough Rosewood Community Association on City-owned land in the Agincourt North community. The garden provides native pollinator habitat while promoting environmental education, biodiversity, volunteer stewardship, and community participation.

The continued maintenance and development of the garden requires modest capital support for on-site garden infrastructure, including water storage capacity and related improvements that support the operation and sustainability of the pollinator garden.

In 2025, City Council enacted By-law 1144-2025, which amended the zoning for the lands at McCowan Road and Finch Avenue. This by-law provides the authority to redirect previously secured Section 37 cash contributions where the funds have not been used for their original intended purpose within three years of the enactment of the original zoning by-law.

The amending by-law specifies that such funds may be redirected at the discretion of the Chief Planner and Executive Director of City Planning, in consultation with the local Councillor, provided the new purpose is identified in the Toronto Official Plan and benefits the community in the vicinity of the subject lands.

As these specific funds have remained unused for more than three years, they are eligible for reallocation. The Rosewood Pollinator Community Garden is located in the Agincourt North community and serves residents in the vicinity of the original development. Allocating these funds to support garden-related capital improvements will enhance City-owned land, support community stewardship and environmental sustainability, and benefit the local community.

This motion seeks to authorize the release of $1,000.00 in eligible Section 37 funds to the Scarborough Rosewood Community Association to support the continued development of the Rosewood Pollinator Community Garden.

Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle, recommends that:

1. M-1539, Blocks B, C, D, E R.P M-1698 (Source Account: XR3026-3700163) as authorized by By-law 1144-2025, to support capital improvements at the Rosewood Pollinator Community Garden.

2026.MM43.49.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to the Laneway Project for Ryerson Avenue Upgrades - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Amber Morley
2026.MM43.49.s:
This Motion seeks Council authority to release $95,000 in Section 37 funds to the Laneway Project for the purpose of funding streetscape and laneway improvements in the area near Ryerson Ave.

An application from the Friends of Alexandra Park group through the Laneway Project coLabs program is proposing to improve and beautify the laneway located adjacent to the Alexandra Hotel and Ryerson Public School. It is an important shared corridor for people with diverse needs and lived experiences.

The laneway was identified by the community as a priority site. It is physically well-suited for activation, wider than most downtown laneways and in relatively good condition, but it is currently underused and impacted by several ongoing challenges including poor lighting, frequent illegal dumping, graffiti and lack of consistent stewardship.

Friends of Alexandra Park is a formalized, energized and organized group with long-term stewardship and community engagement goals for the laneway. This presents a meaningful opportunity to invest in a safer, more welcoming public space that supports positive social interaction and everyday use for residents, families and vulnerable populations alike. This funding will support the installation of planting, lighting, murals, signage and site improvements.

2026.MM43.51.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for Fire-Safety Improvements to the Snack Bar at Milliken Park Field House - by Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
2026.MM43.51.s:
The South Asian Cultural Health Association for Youth and Seniors operates the TRUPTI Social Café at Milliken Park Field House in its snack bar space under a licence agreement. A commercial kitchen fire suppression system is required to support safe and code-compliant on-site food preparation and enhance the facility’s capacity to deliver community food programming.

Section 37 funds secured from the development at 5789 to 5951 Steeles Avenue East were originally allocated toward the expansion of Milliken Park Community Recreation Centre. A portion of these funds remains unspent.

By-law 1145-2025 permits the unused funds to be redirected to another purpose at the discretion of the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, in consultation with the local Councillor, provided that the purpose is identified in the Toronto Official Plan and benefits the community in the vicinity of the source lands.

The proposed fire suppression system is a capital improvement to an existing facility within the same park as Milliken Park Community Recreation Centre. The improvement is consistent with Policies 5.1.1.6(d) and 3.2.2.1(a) and (b) of the Toronto Official Plan, which identify non-profit community facilities as eligible Section 37 community benefits and support the preservation and improvement of local community service facilities.

The facility that includes the snack bar is located in the vicinity of the development at 5789 to 5951 Steeles Avenue East and serves residents of the surrounding community. The proposed capital improvement will enhance the safe and functional use of the facility for services for the community.

This motion seeks authorization to release $8,000 in eligible Section 37 funds to City of Toronto Parks and Recreation for the capital purchase of a commercial kitchen fire suppression system for the licensee’s use to provide service to the community in the snack bar facility at Milliken District Park through a standard City undertaking.

2026.MM43.52.t: Supporting the Realization of the Tamil Community Centre  - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Neethan Shan
2026.MM43.52.s:
Toronto’s Tamil community is nearing a historic moment. Thanks to relentless hard work, the dream of beginning construction on its community centre is fast becoming a reality.

Once completed, the Tamil Community Centre will be a multi-purpose facility serving the Tamil community and the broader Morningside Heights and northeast Scarborough communities. The centre will include a gymnasium, indoor walking track, auditorium, library, museum and archival space, multipurpose programming rooms, outdoor sports facilities, and space for social, educational, cultural and mental health programming.

The Tamil Community Centre represents a generational opportunity to support Toronto's vibrant Tamil community, and Scarborough more broadly. It will be a key addition to the City's network of community and recreation spaces.The Centre has been designed not only as a home for Toronto's Tamil community, but also as a shared community asset. Through a Community Access Agreement with the City, the Centre will provide opportunities for residents of the surrounding neighbourhood, and across the city, to benefit from its spaces and programming.

Since its inception, the City has been a proud partner of the Tamil Community Centre. That partnership has included material support, such as approving a long-term nominal lease for City-owned land and waiving planning application fees to help facilitate development. While the City of Toronto contributed the land, the project has been made possible through strong collaboration between all three orders of government and the community. In 2021, the Government of Canada and the Province of Ontario announced more than $26 million in funding toward construction through the Investing in Canada Infrastructure Program.

The project is at a critical juncture where further City support can help ensure its timely success. Scarborough Community Council unanimously endorsed the Tamil Community Centre’s Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment (SC33.5). This motion seeks Council support for changes to the term of the Tamil Community Centre’s lease and to authorize the waiver of its site plan application fees.
2026.MM43.52.r:
Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Neethan Shan, recommends that:

1. City Council authorize amending the ground lease between the City, as the Landlord, and the Tamil Community Centre, as the Tenant, for part of the south parcel of the City-owned property at 251 Staines Road (formerly addressed 311 Staines Road) originally dated February 15, 2022, and as amended on July 1, 2023 and July 1, 2024, to add a second extension option of ten years less one day on the same terms and conditions as the first extension option, including nominal basic rent, such that the total term inclusive of options of the ground lease is for a total of 49 years less a day, and on such other terms and conditions to be agreed between the Landlord and the Tenant, as may be approved by the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management, and in a form satisfactory to the City Solicitor.

2. City Council authorize the waiver of City development application fees for a Site Plan Control application set out in Schedule 13, Appendix C in Municipal Code Chapter 441 that would otherwise be payable by the Tamil Community Centre to the City for the property located at 251 Staines Road (formerly addressed 311 Staines Road).

2026.MM43.55.t: Expanding Parkland to Serve Liberty Village - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
2026.MM43.55.s:
Liberty Village is a unique Downtown neighbourhood generally bounded by King Street West and Douro Street to the north, the rail tracks to the south, Dufferin Street to the west and Strachan Avenue to the east. The eastern portion of Liberty Village is characterized by mixed-used residential developments with retail, townhouses, and residential towers. The western portion has a concentration of industrial heritage buildings which contribute to the neighbourhood’s distinct character and support a vibrant concentration of commercial, retail and cultural uses.

Much of Liberty Village falls within an Area of Parkland Need as defined by the City’s Parkland Strategy. Parkland provision rates are expected to decline over time in this neighbourhood as residential growth continues.

Limited inventory and competitive market conditions have posed challenges for acquiring new parkland and expanding existing parks within this Downtown area. The City should actively pursue opportunities for new partnerships and creative solutions for growing the parkland network in Liberty Village.

The recommendation in this motion aligns with the objectives of the Council-adopted Official Plan Amendment 914 (Liberty For All Regeneration Area Study), the Garrison Common North Secondary Plan and Liberty Village Public Realm Strategy.

1. City Council direct the General Manager, Parks and Recreation and the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management to explore all opportunities to pursue the expansion of new parkland in Liberty Village, including the acquisition of unused or underutilized nearby adjacent properties to City-owned lands.

2026.MM43.56.t: Improving Coordination Closures to Fight Congestion - by Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll
2026.MM43.56.s:
A significant contributing factor to congestion in the City of Toronto is due to construction and maintenance work to repair, maintain or expand our transit, roads and regional transportation assets.

This spring and summer, residents and visitors to the City had contrasting experiences when dealing with congestion. During Mother’s Day, the City was difficult to navigate due to sections of the Toronto Transit Commission’s subway network and Don Valley Parkway being concurrently closed for maintenance, road closures to accommodate cultural events and sporting competitions, as well as closures on the UP Express operated by Metrolinx. On the other hand, during the six FIFA 2026 match games held in Toronto the City implemented an incredibly successful transportation and mobility plan through improved coordination of local and regional transit services, road and highway closures, and so on.

This motion supports the Chief Congestion Officer and General Manager Transportation Services to utilize a transit focused approach when consulting and planning with the Toronto Transit Commission, other City departments and regional transportation agencies about upcoming closures this year and in future years.
