Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll, recommends that:

1. City Council request the Chief Congestion Officer and the Executive Director, Strategic Capital Coordination Office and the General Manager, Transportation Services, to continue collaborating with Toronto Transit Commission officials to consider planned Toronto Transit Commission subway and streetcar closures and diversions as part of existing transportation network coordination activities, alongside other planned municipal and regional construction projects, significant cultural, entertainment and/or sporting events, and other activities affecting the transportation network, and work with the Toronto Transit Commission and other regional transportation partners to support coordination, proactively identify potential conflicts and overlaps, develop appropriate mitigation measures where feasible, and identify additional resources if needed as part of the next Congestion Management Plan update.

2. City Council request the City Manager, in consultation with the Chief of Police and the Chief Executive Officer, Toronto Transit Commission, to review policies and procedures to improve situational decision-making during major events to help ensure the smooth movement of Toronto Transit Commission surface vehicles.

2026.MM43.57.t: Expanding Parkland to Serve the Growing King-Spadina and Wellington Place Neighbourhoods - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
2026.MM43.57.s:
The King-Spadina area is a diverse and growing Downtown neighbourhood roughly between Bathurst Street to Simcoe Street and Richmond Street West to Front Street West, which includes the long-standing Wellington Place neighbourhood. Overall, King-Spadina has experienced a significant increase in residential population growth over the past ten years and continues to hold a concentration of businesses and jobs, arts and culture destinations, and significant heritage resources.

The entire King-Spadina neighbourhood falls within an Area of Parkland Need as defined by the City’s Parkland Strategy. Parkland provision rates in this neighbourhood are very low, between 0.9 to 3.9 square metres per person. The city-wide average for parkland provision is 28 square metres per person. Parkland provision rates in the King-Spadina Area are expected to decline as growth continues.

Limited inventory, competitive market conditions, built-up urban form, and small parcel fabrics have presented challenges for acquiring new parkland and expanding existing parks within this area. The City should actively pursue opportunities for new partnerships and creative solutions for growing the parkland network in the King-Spadina neighbourhood.

The recommendation in this motion aligns with the objectives of the in-force King Spadina Secondary Plan, King Spadina Heritage Conservation District and the Downtown Plan, as well as the Council-adopted King Spadina Public Realm Strategy and Downtown Parks and Public Realm Plan.
2026.MM43.57.r:

1. City Council direct the General Manager, Parks and Recreation and the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management, in consultation with the General Manager, Economic Development and Culture, to explore opportunities to deliver new parkland and community space within the King-Spadina area to serve rapidly growing residential and employment populations in this Downtown neighbourhood.

2026.MM43.58.t: Planning for Curbside Management when Autonomous Vehicles Arrive - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.58.s:
Many Toronto Councillors already receive complaints about inadequate curbside loading space for both passengers and cargo. These complaints may be about to become much more intense. Around the world, autonomous vehicles are increasingly being used to deliver passengers and cargo. These vehicles can offer safety and cost advantages, but they can also exacerbate congestion and the competition for curb space.

Experts are therefore recommending that cities should start to plan how they will manage the curbside demands of autonomous vehicles.

2026.MM43.59.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Heritage Toronto for Production and Installation of a Plaque Commemorating Monica Lewis - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
2026.MM43.59.s:
In the late 1960’s, Monica Lewis and her husband George bought a property at 1553 Eglinton West and began a lifetime of serving the Caribbean community in Toronto and most of Southern Ontario.

The couple migrated from England as skilled workers with a British education. Lewis’ business, known as Monica’s, first opened as a record store, selling vinyl records, record players, CDs, posters and other electronics. It became a community hub for music enthusiasts and collectors as the store’s collection included sounds popular in the United Kingdom.

In the 1980s, Monica’s became a beauty and cosmetics salon and store that still sold the occasional record. It remained a hub for the community and drew women from all around Southern Ontario as it was one of the few Black hair stores catering to the ever-growing Black population.

Although it closed due to the pandemic and economic pressures from disruptive light rail transit construction, a visit to Monica’s is a fond memory for many residents and frequent visitors of the community. Many recall visiting for a record or just some conversation with Miss Monica, as she was often known.

Monica Lewis died May 20, 2026. The Heritage Toronto plaque will commemorate the cultural and community significance of Lewis' business to Little Jamaica and beyond.
2026.MM43.59.r:

City Council increase the 2026 Operating Budget for Heritage Toronto on a one-time basis by $10,000.00 gross, $0 net, fully funded by Section 37 community benefits obtained from the development at 1603 Eglinton Avenue West (Source Account: XR3026-3700865), secured for community benefits, for the production and installation of a plaque commemorating the entrepreneur Monica Lewis in the Little Jamaica neighbourhood (Cost Centre: HG0001).

2026.MM43.60.t: Renaming a City Park in Honour of Daniel Stopnicki - by Councillor Mike Colle, seconded by Councillor James Pasternak
2026.MM43.60.s:
Daniel Stopnicki was a beloved resident of Eglinton-Lawrence who was tragically killed in April 2026. He was a beloved husband, a cherished son, a dear brother, and a great companion. He was a dedicated teacher and mentor who was beloved and respected by those who knew him.

Daniel is remembered as an enthusiastic and ambitious innovator in real time interactive media, leading numerous exciting companies as Chief Technology and Innovation Officer, and as a dedicated teacher and mentor to many students during his time as a professor and coordinator at Seneca Polytechnic and Centennial College.

In his own neighbourhood, Daniel was a beloved and admired member of his community and was a local hero championing a grassroots campaign to create an off-leash park for his human and canine friends.

Daniel’s father, Roberto, was a longtime City of Toronto employee, serving as a Director in the Transportation Services Division.

To honour Daniel’s memory and his love for his local parks and neighbours, we propose studying options to name a suitable local park asset, where appropriate, in Daniel’s memory. My office will work with local residents and Parks and Recreation staff to work within the city’s Commemorative Framework.

2026.MM43.62.t: Merton Street Streetscape Improvements - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.62.s:
Merton Street, from Yonge Street to Mount Pleasant Road, is experiencing a convergence of pressures driven by concentrated construction activity and shifting traffic patterns. The street supports a diverse and unique mix of residential, and businesses uses, including facilities for seniors, individuals with disabilities and a daycare. Situated close to Davisville TTC Station, the Beltline Trail and Mount Pleasant Cemetery, Merton Street also serves as a key connector to local green spaces, cycling infrastructure, and transit.

As mobility patterns along Merton Street continue to shift, residents have increasingly raised concerns with pedestrian safety, citing narrow sidewalks, limited sightlines, unsafe mid-block crossings, and a need for enhanced wayfinding. While some public realm improvements will be delivered through development applications as part of the Midtown Public Realm Strategy (2022), this motion seeks to address the gaps along the street with the goal of creating a unified and safe corridor.

This motion requests that Transportation Services engage in consultation with the Merton Street community, between Yonge Street and Mount Pleasant Road, and report back in the fourth quarter of 2027 with recommendations for streetscape improvements that can be delivered through future short-term quick-build installations and bundled into broader capital projects and development applications.

Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, recommends that:

1. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services, in consultation with the Executive Director, Development Review, Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, local residents, and the local Councillors’ office to report back in the fourth quarter of 2027 with recommendations for streetscape improvements along Merton Street, between Yonge Street and Mount Pleasant Road, in line with the vision identified in Midtown Parks and Public Realm Plan (2018) and Midtown Public Realm Implementation Strategy (2022).

2026.MM43.63.t: Improving the Development Review Process for Faster Housing Delivery - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Jamaal Myers
2026.MM43.63.s:
Toronto is in a housing crisis. The City has committed to a target of 285,000 new homes by 2031 and must deliver the municipal services that support housing approvals in a timely, predictable and accountable manner. This is especially true for affordable housing, where delays add costs that non-profit builders cannot absorb, and for the parks, community facilities and other public benefits that developments deliver alongside new homes.

Significant progress has been made speeding up approvals in recent years. In April 2024, the City launched the Development Review Division, consolidating approximately 400 staff from across the organization into a single division with a clear mandate. As reported in EX25.2, statutory review timelines for complex applications improved by over 80 percent compared to the previous five-year average. The Division has adopted published Customer Service Standards with target timelines for each application type, launched the File Circulation Tool in March 2025 to modernize how staff conduct reviews, and reports quarterly to the Planning and Housing Committee on development review timelines. The changes that were made clearly delivered improved accountability structures and streamlined processes.

However, fundamental challenges remain in parts of the development process that fall outside the Development Review Division but play a critical role in housing delivery. Staff in Corporate Real Estate Management, Legal Services, Transportation Services, Toronto Water, Parks and Recreation, City Planning, and other divisions can significantly impact timelines. These divisions sit across multiple service areas and their development-related functions are often not covered by service standards or fully defined inter-departmental processes.

There are many examples. The acquisition or conveyance of public laneways (see MM40.42), the negotiation and execution of tieback and crane swing agreements, road occupancy approvals, servicing reviews, and construction staging on lands designated for future parks all require coordination across divisions. Too often, applicants are often left without answers from City staff, facing carrying costs and financing uncertainty that delay or jeopardize the delivery of housing.

The Development Review Division's own Customer Service Standards acknowledge this gap by committing the Division to work with its divisional partners across the City administration to strengthen internal alignment with its service commitments. Critically, these divisions sit outside the control of Development Review and solving these challenges requires a corporate-wide focus.

Timelines can also be highly dependent on applicant-side factors, specifically the quality and timing of submitted materials, compliance with applicable policies and legislation, and clear communication.

This motion does not prescribe organizational restructuring, nor does it suggest that further restructuring is necessarily appropriate. Rather, it requests that the City Manager consult with industry partners to identify ways to improve coordination across the range of service areas involved in the development process, and to offer standardized solutions to issues concerning the acquisition or conveyance of public laneways, the negotiation and execution of tieback and crane swing agreements, road occupancy approvals, servicing reviews, and const…
2026.MM43.63.r:
Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Jamaal Myers, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the Deputy City Manager, Development and Growth Services and the Deputy City Managers responsible for relevant service areas to engage and meet with relevant internal and external stakeholders to identify current processes and practices which impact the timely delivery and cost of housing, and develop standardized solutions to the identified issues, including proposed processes and service standards to address acquisition or conveyance of public laneways, the negotiation and execution of tieback and crane swing agreements, road occupancy approvals, servicing reviews, and construction staging on lands designated for future parks, among others.

2. City Council direct the Deputy City Manager, Development and Growth Services and the Deputy City Managers responsible for relevant service areas, to report through the Planning and Housing Committee in the second quarter of 2027 on the work completed further to Recommendation 1.

2026.MM43.65.t: 29 Church Street - Discontinuing City of Toronto Residential Collection Services - by Councillor Frances Nunziata, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
2026.MM43.65.s:
The purpose of this motion is to address longstanding waste management issues at 29 Church Street, York, which have persisted since 2013 and have progressively worsened over time.

The property is a nine-storey residential apartment building containing 63 dwelling units. As of July 2024, the building received a RentSafeTO score of 82 out of 100, resulting in a "Needs Improvement" classification.

The building's designated waste storage area is located along Church Street, within approximately 30 metres of residential properties to the west and north. The existing waste management infrastructure is insufficient to accommodate the volume of waste generated by the building. Despite twice-weekly municipal waste collection, the available waste storage capacity is inadequate, resulting in chronic overflow, loose garbage accumulating on neighbouring properties and the public right-of-way, and ongoing unsanitary conditions.

The property has experienced persistent rodent activity, including visible burrowing beneath the waste storage area. Nearby residents have repeatedly reported concerns regarding rodent infestations, offensive odours, litter, and the adverse impacts these conditions have on the surrounding neighbourhood.

The ongoing nature of these issues is demonstrated by repeated inspections and enforcement actions by Municipal Licensing and Standards. Recent site inspections identified numerous deficiencies, including damaged waste bins, poor housekeeping practices, and inadequate maintenance of the waste storage area.

This motion seeks to grant the General Manger of Solid Waste Management the authorization the discontinue City of Toronto residential waste collection services.
2026.MM43.65.r:
Councillor Frances Nunziata, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher, recommends that:

1. Council Council direct the Executive Director, Municipal Licensing and Standards and the General Manager, Solid Waste Management Services:

a. to diligently review waste collection issues at 29 Church Street in York from 2016 to the present and consider taking further steps in accordance with the Code and other applicable laws to address waste management concerns at the property; and

b. to report to the Infrastructure and Environment Committee by the end of second quarter of 2027 on whether and how the Code could be amended to authorize City officials to discontinue City collection of waste at properties found to have violated the applicable waste provisions of the Code that require the waste (including organic materials, garbage, yard waste, and certain recycled materials) to be stored in a clean manner to protect against rodents, vermin, pests, litter and other disturbances.

2026.MM43.67.t: Intergovernmental Collaboration to Deliver Transit for Humber Bay Shores - by Councillor Amber Morley, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
2026.MM43.67.s:
Over the last 7 years, City Staff have worked closely with Metrolinx on matters related to the redevelopment of the Christie’s site at Park Lawn Road and Lake Shore Boulevard, the development of a Transportation Master Plan for the broader area, and the design of the planned Park Lawn GO Station.

During the Christie’s planning study work in 2019, City Staff worked with Metrolinx to link the redevelopment of the site to the delivery of the GO Station. This collaboration was important for the City to achieve a positive outcome in negotiations with the developer. Additionally, the redevelopment of the site, along with the development in the broader Humber Bay Shores area, were important factors in building a business case for the GO Station.

At the June 2026 Planning and Housing Committee meeting, Staff shared that the developer has paused their plans for the Christie’s site and as a result, the future of the Park Lawn GO Station remains unclear.

I have continued to meet with City Staff, Metrolinx and the developer to find a way forward. The City and Metrolinx both recognize the importance of improving transit service, including GO service, to this growing area of South Etobicoke. A formalized working group would ensure that all parties remain at the table and can effectively collaborate on delivering improved transit to Humber Bay Shores and the surrounding area.
2026.MM43.67.r:
Councillor Amber Morley, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow, recommends that:

1. City Council, further to its decision on item 2025.EX27.4, request the Provincial government and Metrolinx to form a working group with City Officials, Staff, the Ministries of Infrastructure, Transportation, Municipal Affairs and Housing, and Finance Officials, and other related parties, to examine ways to advance the development of the Park Lawn GO Station and other transit improvements in Humber Bay Shores, recognizing the existing growth and development in the area.

2026.MM43.69.t: Strengthening Toronto’s Multi-Tenant Houses Framework: Enforcement and Path to Compliance - by Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Vincent Crisanti
2026.MM43.69.s:
Toronto adopted the city-wide Multi-Tenant Houses framework in December 2022, effective March 31, 2024, to establish consistent safety and licensing standards, preserve deeply affordable housing, and provide a pathway for previously unlicensed multi-tenant houses to enter legal, regulated operation.

Since implementation, Municipal Licensing and Standards, in collaboration with the Housing Secretariat, Toronto Fire Services, Toronto Building and other City divisions, has undertaken significant work to implement the framework, process licence applications, support operators through the licensing process, and coordinate compliance and enforcement activities.

As implementation continues, City Council would benefit from additional information on how key components of the framework are operating in practice. This Motion requests updates on implementation activities, including the operational use of existing enforcement tools and the effectiveness of implementation supports, such as the Multi-Tenant Houses Renovation Program and the Operator Concierge Service, in assisting operators through the licensing process.

The requested reports are intended to inform Council's understanding of the framework's implementation and identify opportunities for continuous improvement.

2026.MM43.70.t: Ensuring Community Protections and Electrification Commitments for the Bloor-Lansdowne GO Station - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
2026.MM43.70.s:
The Province’s transit agency, Metrolinx, is leading the expansion of the Barrie GO Line, including the construction of the new Bloor-Lansdowne GO station located south of Bloor Street and west of Lansdowne Avenue.

When Metrolinx’s plans to run electrified rail service along the Barrie line were put on indefinite hold, significant gaps in infrastructure protection became evident for residents living south of Bloor Street along the Barrie GO corridor. While noise barriers are in place along nearby sections of the corridor, no barriers are proposed for the densely populated residential stretch immediately adjacent to the new station.

Noise and vibration mitigation is particularly important at the station location because trains will idle while passengers embark and disembark, and locomotive sounds, vibration, and emissions will rise as trains exit the station. Train service along this section of the line is projected to significantly increase in the coming years, with trains entering or exiting the station in either direction every 7.5 minutes, leading to increased noise and diesel exhaust from the locomotives, and loud bell ringing (over 70 decibels) from approaching trains.

The Bloor-Lansdowne GO station is adjacent to a number of residential communities, with some residents in very close proximity to the new station. Many in the surrounding community are supportive of transit expansion, but infrastructure expansion must not come at the expense of local residents’ health and quality of life.

Metrolinx already uses noise walls and bell mitigation strategies across other parts of its network. This motion requests that the Province and Metrolinx apply these standard mitigation tools equally to the Davenport community to protect neighbours from the impacts of expanded diesel rail service, and that Metrolinx upholds a commitment to full line electrification.
2026.MM43.70.r:
Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher, recommends that:

1. City Council request Metrolinx to install noise barrier walls along the Barrie GO corridor south of Bloor Street, appropriately sized for current and projected GO diesel locomotive traffic volumes, and consistent with adjacent properties along the Barrie corridor.

2. City Council request Metrolinx to develop and implement a train bell mitigation plan and other point-of-emission mitigations for the Bloor-Lansdowne GO Station, and every station along the Barrie GO line in the City of Toronto, to ensure safe, quiet rail operations.

3. City Council request the Ontario Minister of Transportation to accelerate the electrification of the Barrie GO line to eliminate diesel pollution and lower engine noise impact for local residents, and to provide a commitment and confirmed timeline for full electrification.

4. City Council request Metrolinx to expedite its assessment of noise mitigation requirements for the Bloor–Lansdowne GO Station and construct them before the station opens and prior to the implementation of expanded train service.

2026.MM43.71.t: 404 Rustic Road - Request for City Solicitor to Attend at the Toronto Local Appeal Body - by Councillor Frances Nunziata, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher

The proposed garden suite is approximately 29.5 percent larger than what the by-law permits.

On June 25, 2026, the Etobicoke York District Panel of the Committee of Adjustment approved the Application (the “Decision”). A copy of the Decision is attached as Attachment 1. The last date of appeal was July 15, 2026.

For the City to continue to effectively assess its case, the City Solicitor requires the expertise of an external consultant to advise on the Applicant’s proposed plan, and to potentially make recommendations respecting a solution.

This Motion will authorize the City Solicitor to appeal the Decision to the Toronto Local Appeal Body and to resolve the matter on behalf of the City in their discretion.

2026.MM43.72.t: Assessing the Impact of the Data Centre located at 48 Lowe’s Place - by Councillor Vincent Crisanti, seconded by Councillor Stephen Holyday
2026.MM43.72.s:

More recently, residents in the surrounding area have raised concerns regarding the data centre’s potential impact on the community, including water consumption, hydro use, and noise.

Recognizing the need for stronger oversight as more data centres emerge across the City, I supported a Member Motion (MM39.47) asking staff to develop a process to address the impact of data centres in Toronto, ensuring that they better reflect the needs of the local community.

Considering these recent concerns, I am requesting city staff urgently meet with the applicant to consider additional measures to mitigate residents’ concerns regarding this site.

2026.MM43.73.t: Reimagining the Future of the Former Ontario Science Centre Public Consultation Report - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Jon Burnside
2026.MM43.73.s:
This report presents the findings of a community engagement process undertaken in Spring 2026 to reimagine the future of the former Ontario Science Centre site at 770 Don Mills Road. Informed by this public feedback, the report puts forward a community-informed vision for the site's revitalization, re-opening, and return to public use.

This report and engagement process has been led by Save Ontario’s Science Centre, Moriyama Teshima Architects, Councillor Josh Matlow, and Councillor Jon Burnside, and was carried out under the direction of motions approved by City Council including 2024.MM22.3.

In April 2023, the Provincial government announced its decision to relocate the Ontario Science Centre to the waterfront, and in June 2024 it abruptly closed the building. The province's own engineering consultants recommended repairing the building rather than closing it, and offers of professional and philanthropic support to fund the work followed. Despite several Council approved motions requesting provincial engagement on the site, the Province has yet to share details of its plans.

The purpose of the community engagement was not to revisit the relocation decision or to evaluate specific redevelopment proposals. Rather, the process sought to identify the public values, priorities, and principles that should guide the future of this significant public asset, and to consider how its educational, environmental, cultural, architectural, and civic contributions can continue to serve communities across Toronto and Ontario.

Any future plans for the site must be grounded in community priorities. The consultations therefore engaged the residents of Flemingdon Park and Thorncliffe Park directly, the communities closest to the site and most affected by its closure, along with residents from across Toronto, to hear their vision for a re-imagined 770 Don Mills Road. Key themes that emerged included continued public use of the site, multiple purposes including learning and discovery, access to the ravine and surrounding green space, the architectural significance of the building, and priorities for community and cultural programming.

This attached report proposes next steps to help determine a sustainable future use of the site that ensures public benefit and access. It recommends that any process to determine the future use and vision for the site, including determining future governance and funding options, brings the province together with the City, federal government, community members, and institutional and philanthropic partners.

Critically, this will require the provincial government to engage on the future of the site in good faith. This report offers the province a positive, community-grounded starting point: a path forward shaped by residents, design professionals, and city-builders who share the goal of seeing this site thrive again.

The consultation findings ultimately demonstrate that 770 Don Mills Road is a significant public asset whose value lies in the intersection of learning, landscape, architecture, culture, and community. The message from participants is clear: the use of the site may change, but its public purpose should endure. The next chapter of 770 Don Mills Road should build on that legacy, creating a place where learning, discovery, and connection continue to shape Ontario's future.

2026.MM43.77.t: Advancing Digital Sovereignty for the City of Toronto - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Lily Cheng
2026.MM43.77.s:
On June 4, 2026, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Evan Solomon launched "AI for All," Canada's new national artificial intelligence strategy. The strategy commits over $2.3 billion in federal spending over five years, anchored in three guiding principles – Trust, Opportunity, and Sovereignty. Through this strategy, the federal government aims to strengthen Canada’s AI sovereignty by supporting globally competitive Canadian AI companies to ensure that AI systems are developed and governed on Canadian terms.

In November 2025, the Government of Canada published the Digital Sovereignty Framework, an approach for improving digital readiness at the Government of Canada. This framework defines digital sovereignty as the Government of Canada’s ability to exercise autonomy over its digital infrastructure, data, and intellectual property, and the capacity to operate effectively and make independent decisions about its digital assets, regardless of where technologies are developed, hosted, or supported.

For the City of Toronto, these developments present an opportunity to consider a strong, homegrown approach to sovereignty over digital infrastructure, including data and artificial intelligence – one that balances reliance on foreign-owned technology, prioritizes Canadian solutions, and aligns with federal efforts.

Recently, international municipalities such as Copenhagen and Aarhus, Denmark's two largest cities, and Amsterdam, the Dutch capital, have shared plans and taken preliminary steps towards greater digital sovereignty, often through a phased or pilot approach, including replacing Microsoft products with open-source software or other non-US alternatives. These initial measures are aimed at reducing reliance on US-owned technology providers in the long-term, citing reasons such as rising costs, risks to reliance on a single vendor, geopolitical risks, and concerns about potential for service disruption if international relations deteriorate.
2026.MM43.77.r:
Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Lily Cheng, recommends that:

1. City Council request the Government of Canada to engage with the City of Toronto, including Technology Services, the Chief Procurement Officer, the Chief Information Security Officer, and the City Clerk to identify opportunities to advance municipal digital sovereignty in alignment with Canada’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, including dedicated funding to support municipalities in transitioning to Canadian-based technology and software solutions.

2. City Council forward this Item to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities for their consideration and advocacy.

2026.MM43.78.t: Advancing Local Priorities in Thorncliffe Park - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
2026.MM43.78.s:
Thorncliffe Park is a densely populated and culturally diverse community and has long served as an important area of arrival for newcomers to Toronto. Currently, the community is undergoing significant change associated with major transit investments, including the Ontario Line and the planned Transit-Oriented Community surrounding the future Thorncliffe Park Station. City staff and the local Councillor’s office have recently engaged with the Urban Land Institute and local stakeholders to consider how the City can optimize the benefits of these investments, and several opportunities have emerged from these discussions around delivering new housing, jobs, community facilities, parks, public spaces, and improving connections within and beyond the neighbourhood.

This engagement process has identified that, as Thorncliffe Park continues to grow, there is a need for a coordinated approach that builds on the community’s strengths and addresses mobility, connectivity, and public realm challenges. This includes improving walking, cycling, and transit connections; enhancing parks, open spaces, and community gathering places; creating safer, more accessible and welcoming streets and public spaces; and strengthening neighbourhood identity, social cohesion, and local economic vitality.

A coordinated implementation approach is needed to help advance these priorities and ensure residents benefit from ongoing investments while maintaining Thorncliffe Park as a vibrant and welcoming community.

1. City Council direct the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, in collaboration with other City Divisions, as appropriate, to determine priorities and implementation mechanisms for enhancements to the public realm and streetscape, multi-modal transportation connections and other initiatives to support a growing population in Thorncliffe Park, including through the following actions:

a. continued collaboration with Metrolinx and Infrastructure Ontario on the planning, design and delivery of transit infrastructure and Transit-Oriented Communities within Thorncliffe Park to advance mobility, connectivity, place-making and community benefits and identify opportunities for the activation and long-term stewardship of publicly accessible spaces associated with the Ontario Line infrastructure, including the lands beneath the guideway.

2. City Council direct the General Manager, Parks and Recreation and other appropriate City Divisions, to ensure the needs of Thorncliffe Park’s growing population through Parks and Recreation’s facilities and capital planning process.

3. City Council direct the General Manager, Economic Development and Culture and other appropriate City Divisions, to consider opportunities to support and engage local businesses and community agencies to ensure economic development and commercial vitality in Thorncliffe Park.

4. City Council direct the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, to report to the North York Community Council in the second quarter of 2027 on the matters identified in Recommendation 1.

2026.MM43.79.t: Exploring Alternative Options to Clarify Complex Intersections - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe
2026.MM43.79.s:
Maintaining clarity and understanding of road rules is essential to ensuring safety for all road users. In some areas of the City, road configurations make this challenging. In Don Valley West, the intersection of Bayview Avenue and Bayview Heights Drive is signed “Do Not Block the Intersection” for northbound traffic – however, the intersection is commonly blocked as the area referred to by the sign is not immediately obvious. This makes it nearly impossible for drivers looking to turn north onto Bayview Avenue from Bayview Heights Drive to find a gap, and necessitates drivers to act quickly when a gap does appear, increasing the risk of accidents. On a stretch of road which has already seen several serious collisions in recent years, the present condition is untenable.

Denoting the intersection through pavement markings or other indicators would ensure greater clarity for drivers, improving the condition for north-turning traffic from Bayview Heights Drive and improving road safety in the area. This is just one example of many in a City with many complicated intersections that would benefit from clearer design for road users.

Toronto should be exploring all options to improve road safety. While the types of signage and pavement markings available to us are defined by the Highway Traffic Act, Toronto should look to neighbours operating under the same legislative constraints to adapt best practices in our own road design and traffic operations.
2026.MM43.79.r:
Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe, recommends that:

1. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services, to undertake a jurisdictional scan for alternative Highway Traffic Act-compliant pavement markings and other options utilized in Ontario municipalities to denote ambiguous intersections for the purpose of increasing driver safety and awareness and to prevent “box blocking”, and report back to the Infrastructure and Environment Committee on findings in the first quarter of 2027.

2026.MM43.80.t: Authorization to Release Section 42 Funds - Collaborating with the Friends of Allan Gardens on the Development of the Greenhouse Link Building - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik
2026.MM43.80.s:
Allan Gardens is one of Toronto's oldest and most cherished public spaces. Open to the public since 1860, it is a rare downtown commons that has remained open and accessible to all Torontonians across generations, and holds deep cultural and civic significance for the city. As outlined in the Allan Gardens’ Refresh: A Vision Document for Allan Gardens (2017) and the Growing with the City: An Ecosystem of Initiatives for Allan Gardens (2023), a comprehensive vision has been established to expand and modernize the park's conservatory infrastructure and outdoor garden spaces.

The proposed Greenhouse Link Building, advanced by the Friends of Allan Gardens, would double the conservatory's footprint from its current 16,000 square feet to over 32,000 square feet, positioning it among the largest conservatories in North America. The project has generated significant public and philanthropic support: a community petition has gathered more than 7,000 signatures, and substantial commitments from private philanthropists toward the expansion, contingent on public funding contributions.

This motion directs the dedication of $9 million of locally available funds to further the Allan Gardens Master Plan and the Greenhouse Link Building, in addition to funds allocated through Council Direction in May 2026. Additionally, it directs staff to collaborate with the Friends of Allan Gardens on this transformational project and provide an update report in 2027 regarding the design, funding strategy operating model and any recommended agreements. The Allan Gardens Conservatory will in perpetuity remain free for the public to use.

2026.MM43.82.t: Supporting Employment Uses through the Review of the Former City of Scarborough Employment Districts Zoning By-law in Scarborough North - by Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
2026.MM43.82.s:
Ward 23 contains a significant concentration of lands designated as Employment Areas in the Toronto Official Plan. Many of these lands, including some employment districts that extend across the ward boundary, remain subject to former City of Scarborough Employment Districts Zoning By-law Number 24982.

Legacy use definitions, permissions, performance standards and site-specific exceptions can create uncertainty for businesses seeking to establish, adapt or expand employment uses on these lands. These provisions may not clearly reflect contemporary business operations or align with the current Official Plan and provincial policy framework for Employment Areas.

The City’s Phase 2 Zoning Conformity for Official Plan Employment Areas work program provides an appropriate opportunity to examine these issues. This motion requests that City Planning specifically consider zoning challenges affecting lands subject to By-law Number 24982 that are wholly or partially within Ward 23, and identify appropriate changes, guidance or other measures through the City’s existing conformity and harmonization work.

The objective is to provide business owners, City staff, planners and decision-makers with clear and accurate information about how the legacy zoning framework interacts with the Toronto Official Plan and recent provincial changes. Greater clarity will help businesses make more timely and informed decisions about locating, adapting or expanding their operations, while supporting more consistent assessments, clearer planning and zoning requirements, and the long-term protection and promotion of the employment function of these lands.

1. City Council request the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, in consultation with the General Manager, Economic Development and Culture, or their delegates, to include, as part of reporting on Phase 2 of the Zoning Conformity for Official Plan Employment Areas work program, consideration of and appropriate recommendations to address zoning challenges affecting businesses seeking to establish, adapt or expand employment uses on lands wholly or partially within Ward 23 that are subject to former City of Scarborough Employment Districts Zoning By-law Number 24982.

2026.MM43.83.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for the Reconstruction of Church Street in Coordination with Water Main Replacement - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik
2026.MM43.83.s:
The Church-Wellesley Village Business Improvement Area sits at the geographic and cultural heart of Canada's largest LGBTQ2S+ neighbourhood. Known as The Village, this vibrant and diverse community is bordered by Bloor Street to the north, Carlton Street to the south, Jarvis Street to the east, and Yonge Street to the west. The Business Improvement Area itself is bound by Gloucester Street to the north and Wood Street to the south, with its east-west boundaries encompassing the immediate mixed-use and residential properties along Church Street. For decades, The Village has served as a gathering place for diverse communities, a primary point of contact for tourists, and a welcoming destination for LGBTQ2S+ newcomers to Toronto. It is home to several major public events throughout the year, most notably the annual Pride Toronto celebration, as well as the Village Fest community event, the Halloween on Church Festival, and numerous other events of varying scales.

The community has engaged in multiple rounds of consultation over many years and now expects the City to move forward without further delay. In 2014, the State of the Village Study and Neighbourhood Plan was completed following extensive community engagement. In 2019, early discussions around the YongeTOmorrow project included commitments to coordinate the reconstruction of Church Street with the broader reconstruction of Yonge Street. However, the YongeTOmorrow project was first delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and is now further delayed pending completion of the Ontario Line, which is anticipated no earlier than 2030 and potentially as late as 2035 or 2040. Given this extended timeline, the reconstruction of Church Street must be advanced independently and without further deferral.

Adding urgency to this matter, watermain replacement work originally scheduled for Church Street — from Gloucester Street south to Carlton Street — was deliberately deferred in 2021 so that it could be coordinated with a full streetscape reconstruction following the Business Improvement Area's finalization and approval of a Streetscape Master Plan. That watermain infrastructure is now overdue for replacement and there are short segments in critical condition that must proceed in advance of road reconstruction in order to prevent recurring watermain breaks and sink holes.

In 2026, extensive community engagement through the Church Street Pedestrianization Pilot surfaced clear and consistent design priorities to guide the revitalization of Church Street. These include the addition of patio space to support local businesses, widened sidewalks to improve pedestrian movement and accessibility, the installation of permanent vehicle mitigation infrastructure to facilitate street closures for festivals, events, and pedestrianization, as well as enhanced seating, trees and planting, lighting, public art, and waste receptacle installations throughout the corridor.

This motion directs the Deputy City Manager of Infrastructure Services, whose portfolio includes Transportation Services, Toronto Water, and Engineering and Construction Services, to advance a phased approach to the construction required for Church Street from Gloucester Street south to Carlton Street, proceeding first in 2027 with the critical segments of water main replacement previously deferred, while advancing a strategy for the upcoming reconstruction of Church Street that delivers on the vision of the Church-Wellesley Village Streetscape Master Plan, in a manner that is efficient, financially prudent, and reflects the community's vision and infrastructure priorities identified through years of consultation.

2026.MM43.84.s:
Main Sewage Treatment Playground is an 11.2-hectare park at Eastern Avenue and Emdaabimok Avenue that features a range of sports amenities, including purpose-built, tournament sized pickleball courts, two basketball courts, a rugby field, a baseball diamond and a skatepark.

The Mayor and I have worked with Parks and Recreation staff, Toronto Water staff and local community groups to add these dedicated pickleball courts to ensure equitable and local access to this rapidly growing sport.

This well-used park is located on land owned by Toronto Water and serves as an important community space, especially in the summer months.

The new name should be reflective of the area and the great wide-range facilities available.

Given the proximity to Ashbridge’s Bay Wastewater Treatment Plant and Ashbridge’s Bay Park, I would like to request that City Council rename Main Sewage Treatment Playground to

Ashbridge’s Bay Sports Hub.

Reason for urgency:

The recent opening of the new pickleball courts has highlighted the fact that the current name is unfamiliar to most residents and creates confusion. Clarity is needed for planned events including tournaments.

2026.MM43.85.t: Advancing the Bridletowne Neighbourhood Centre/Community Hub - by Councillor Nick Mantas, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
2026.MM43.85.s:
The Bridletowne Neighbourhood Centre/Community Hub is a long-standing City-building initiative that will bring much-needed community space, programs and services to the Finch-Warden/Steeles-L’Amoreaux/Bridletowne area.

For more than a decade, City Council has supported the use of the City-owned lands at 1355 Bridletowne Circle to create a multi-service community hub. The City acquired the property in 2011 for approximately $5.9 million, and the proposed nominal transfer of the 5.2-acre site to the YMCA of Greater Toronto represents a significant City contribution toward unlocking long-planned community infrastructure in an area of significant need.

While Scarborough Health Network is no longer advancing its component of the project, the YMCA of Greater Toronto remains committed to moving the project forward with United Way Greater Toronto and other community partners.

The Bridletowne Neighbourhood Centre will be an innovative and exciting model featuring two of the City’s leading charities. The updated vision continues to provide important community benefits, including a YMCA with health and fitness services, aquatics, summer day camp, youth and family programming and shared community space, alongside United Way community agency space serving local residents at all ages and stages under one roof.

The revised project continues to advance Council’s original vision for the site: using public land to support community infrastructure in an area of significant need. Proceeding with the nominal transfer of the northerly portion of 1355 Bridletowne Circle to the YMCA will help move this important project forward, while allowing the City to update the transaction documents to reflect the current project structure, protect the public-purpose use of the lands, and preserve flexibility for future municipal needs.

The YMCA of Greater Toronto has been committed to this project since its inception. Advancing this project now brings the residents of the Finch-Warden/Steeles-L’Amoreaux/Bridletowne area an important step closer to having much anticipated recreational and community services in their local community.

Reason for Urgency:

This motion is urgent as the Bridletowne Neighbourhood Centre project would be delayed without adoption of this motion.

3. City Council direct the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management, in consultation with the Chief Executive Officer, CreateTO, the General Manager, Seniors Services and Long-Term Care, and other relevant Divisions, to urgently identify and assess potential City needs for the portion of 1355 Bridletowne Circle over which the City is reserving an interest, including potential Seniors Services and Long-Term Care needs, and to report back as necessary with any recommended next steps.

2026.MM43.86.s:
The Applicant applied to the Committee of Adjustment to request variances from City-wide Zoning By-law 569-2013 (Application A0304/26TEY) to widen the existing driveway. The variances required to By-law 569-2013 included maximum permitted driveway width, front yard landscaping, and front yard soft landscaping. Ahead of the Committee of Adjustment hearing, the Application was revised to remove the variance for front yard soft landscaping.

On June 17, 2026, the Toronto and East York District Panel of the Committee of Adjustment refused the Application. A copy of the Decision is attached as Attachment 1. The Applicant appealed the Decision to the Toronto Local Appeal Body on July 7, 2026.

In a report from the Director of Community Planning, Toronto and East York District dated June 4, 2026, Community Planning Staff raised concerns with respect to the Application and recommended that the Application be refused. In particular, Community Planning Staff opined that landscaped front yards contribute significantly to the quality of the streetscape, tree canopy opportunities, and the overall character of the neighbourhood.

This Motion will authorize the City Solicitor to attend the Toronto Local Appeal Body to uphold the Committee of Adjustment’s refusal of the Application and to resolve the matter on behalf of the City in their discretion.

This matter is urgent as the Application has been appealed to the Toronto Local Appeal Body.

City Council enacted By-law 1567-2025 at its meeting December 16 and 17, 2025, to permit the development.

This motion is required to correct an error identified by Community Planning following the enactment of the By-law 1567-2025. As enacted, Paragraph 7, Regulation (H)(ii) excludes all uses identified in Paragraph 7, Regulation (C) from contributing toward the required minimum non-residential gross floor area. This has the unintended effect of preventing certain institutional uses from counting toward the required 4,500 square metres of non-residential gross floor area.

Community Planning wishes to clarify the non-residential gross floor area requirement, as reflected in the Application and Staff Report considered by City Council. The Application has not changed in any material way from what was considered and approved by City Council.

Community Planning is of the opinion that the revision to By-law 1567-2025, as set out in the Recommendations is appropriate, minor, good planning and does not require any further public notice. There are no other changes to the approved Zoning By-law.

This is an urgent matter as ambiguity in the Zoning By-law may cause undesirable delay in obtaining building permits.

2026.MM43.89.t: Authority to Accept Donations Raised Through Fundraising Campaign for Moss Park Arena Improvements - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
2026.MM43.89.s:
The City is making improvements to Moss Park Arena’s interior, including the washroom, boardroom, snack bar, pro-shop, Zamboni room and multipurpose rooms. Construction at the City-owned facility is expected to take place from June 2027 to May 2028.

Moss Park Arena is one of eight arenas in Toronto that are operated by volunteer Arena Boards of Management (Arena Boards), which are City agencies. The board-run arenas provide indoor ice sport facilities along with programming that can include hockey, figure skating and leisure skating. The Arena Board’s mandate includes:

a. Ensuring the arena is safe, well-maintained and accessible for use by the local community, neighbourhood organizations and others;

b. allocating the use of the arena facility in a way that balances the needs of the local community residents and organizations and user groups; and

c. allocating ice-time to users in consultation with the General Manager of Parks and Recreation.

The Arena Board has expressed a desire to raise funds to augment the project’s existing Parks and Recreation capital budget and $300,000 in Section 37 funding approved by Council through 2026.MM39.23. These additional funds would be used to procure items that are out of scope for the City improvement project but would improve the visitor and user experience and improve operating conditions and efficiency. Working in collaboration, the Arena Board and Parks and Recreation staff have identified items that could be added to the project depending on the success of the fundraising campaign. These include:

a. a new time clock,

b. additional pro-shop upgrades,

c. additional snack bar area improvements,

d. house league office and skating club room improvements,

e. a new Sound system, and

g. second electric Zamboni.

The fundraising campaign target is $238,000. However, individual items cost less (for example, the time clock is an estimated $25,000) and could be purchased depending on available funds. If fundraising targets for specific enhancements are not met, all funds will be dedicated to state of good repair needs for Moss Park Arena.

My office and the Moss Park Arena Board have been working closely to develop a sponsorship package and campaign, and have secured a few large donations to kick start this public campaign to revitalize the arena.

Under the City of Toronto Donation Policy, solicited donations of cash designated for specific purposes will only be accepted by the City where Council has authorized the specific purpose through a philanthropic or fundraising campaign (whether conducted by staff or third parties). The Policy also requires Council authority to accept donations of more than $50,000 from the same donor for the same purpose in a fiscal year. The Policy applies to City divisions as well as agencies including Arena Boards.

Staff and the Arena Board have determined that the City’s existing DonateTO web portal would be an effective mechanism for accepting online donations and issuing tax receipts, as applicable. Parks and Recreation and the City Manager’s Office would work together to onboard this program to the online platform. The City can also accept donations through other means, such as major gifts by cheque. The Arena Board would be responsible for promoting the campaign.

The recommendations in this Motion would provide staff and the Moss Park Arena Board of Management the necessary authority to undertake the philanthropic campaign and to accept funds raised to the Moss Park Arena Improvements capital project.

This motion is urgent in order to start the campaign as soon as possible, as there is no regular meeting of Council until 2027.

1. City Council authorize the Moss Park Arena Board of Management to initiate a fundraising campaign led by the Moss Park Arena Board of Management and to apply the donated funds toward eligible improvements at Moss Park Arena, in compliance with the City of Toronto Donation Policy.

2. City Council authorize the General Manager, Parks and Recreation, to accept and administer donations raised through a fundraising campaign led by the Moss Park Arena Board of Management and to apply the donated funds toward eligible improvements at Moss Park Arena, in compliance with the City of Toronto Donation Policy.

3 City Council direct the Moss Park Arena Board of Management and the General Manager, Parks and Recreation, in consultation with the Chief Financial Officer and Treasurer, to negotiate and execute the necessary agreements in a form satisfactory to the City Solicitor, to facilitate the Moss Park Arena Improvements project fundraising campaign.

4. 2026.MM43.92.t: Weekend and Holiday Standing Prohibition on Barkdene Hills - by Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
2026.MM43.92.s:
Barkdene Hills is a residential street near the Scarborough Bluffs that experiences increased vehicle traffic and parking demand during the spring and summer months, particularly on weekends and public holidays.

Residents have raised concerns that vehicles parked along both sides of the street can restrict traffic flow, reduce visibility, create congestion, and impede access for residents, emergency services, waste collection vehicles, and other municipal services.

Barkdene Hills is also used as a Toronto Transit Commission bus route. As the proposed parking regulation would affect a roadway on which the Toronto Transit Commission operates, the matter is being directed to City Council for consideration.

To help maintain safe and reliable access through the neighbourhood during peak periods, including the continued safe and efficient operation of Toronto Transit Commission service, a seasonal standing prohibition is proposed for the north side of Barkdene Hills, between Brimley Road South and Brooklawn Avenue.

Reason for Urgency:

This matter is urgent because increased summer traffic and parking activity are already occurring, and the resulting congestion may impede emergency access and create immediate safety concerns.

1. City Council prohibit standing from 9:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m., Saturday, Sunday, and public holidays from May 1 to September 30 of each year, on the north side of Barkdene Hills, from Brimley Road South to Brooklawn Avenue.

2026.MM43.94.t: Advancing the Pakistani Canadian Community Centre - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Jon Burnside
2026.MM43.94.s:
Toronto is home to a vibrant Pakistani community, the largest in Canada. More than 160,000 residents of the Greater Toronto Area are of Pakistani origin.

The Pakistani community has a significant population in the eastern part of the City. The community is currently underserved by cultural community facilities and dedicated spaces to support its large and growing population.

The Pakistani Canadian Community Centre Project has been working diligently, together with intergovernmental partners, to advance a plan to deliver a dynamic, multicultural and multi-purpose centralized community center space that also serves residents of the City writ large.

This motion asks City of Toronto staff to explore the possibility of replicating the successful models of the Chinese Cultural Centre of Greater Toronto, and the Tamil Community Centre to support the development of a dedicated Pakistani community centre that is located close to where the majority of the population resides.

This motion is urgent as the Pakistani Canadian Community Centre project would be delayed by the Council Recess.

2026.MM43.95.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds from the Development at 53 to 63 Sheppard Avenue West and 62 to 68 Bogert Avenue for Improvements to the Schoolyard at St. Edward Catholic School - by Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Amber Morley
2026.MM43.95.s:
St. Edward Catholic School, located at 1 Botham Road in Willowdale, serves students, families, and the surrounding community as part of the Toronto Catholic District School Board. The schoolyard is an important outdoor space that supports recreation, physical activity, and community connection for students and local residents.

The school has identified significant challenges with the existing schoolyard, including poor drainage and uneven grading, which result in the field becoming waterlogged and unusable following rainfall. These conditions limit safe outdoor activities for students and reduce opportunities for community recreation. St. Edward Catholic School and its Catholic School Parent Council have proposed improvements to create a properly drained, levelled, and multi-use artificial turf field that would provide a safe and accessible space year-round. The school’s proposal and partnership request are outlined in Attachment 1, dated June 9, 2026.

This motion proposes allocating $50,000 in Section 37 funds from the development at 53 to 63 Sheppard Avenue West and 62 to 68 Bogert Avenue to support capital improvements to the St. Edward Catholic School schoolyard, subject to the Toronto Catholic District School Board entering into a Community Access Agreement with the City of Toronto.

Through this agreement, the improved schoolyard would be available for community use outside of school hours for a period of 20 years, including opportunities for local recreation programming and community activities. This partnership would maximize the use of existing public assets and provide long-term benefits for both students and residents in the surrounding Willowdale neighbourhood.

The City recognizes the importance of working collaboratively with local school boards to improve shared community spaces. Supporting schoolyard improvements is a cost-effective way to expand recreational opportunities, enhance outdoor spaces for children and families, and strengthen connections within the community.

We appreciate the leadership and advocacy of the St. Edward Catholic School community, including Principal Kirsten Kelly and the Parent Council Chair, Nicole Kerr and Co-Chair, Cathy LeBlanc, in advancing this important project. This investment represents an opportunity to transform an underutilized space into a safe, accessible, and valuable community asset.

Reason for Urgency:

This Motion is urgent as the July 29 to 31, 2026 meeting is the last scheduled meeting of City Council before the election period. Approval at this time will provide certainty to the Toronto Catholic District School Board and the St. Edward Catholic School community, enabling the parties to advance discussions on a Community Access Agreement and begin planning for the proposed schoolyard improvements without delay. Deferring consideration would postpone the delivery of a valuable community amenity that will benefit students and Willowdale residents for years to come.

2026.MM43.96.t: Authority to Accept Donations Raised Through Fundraising Campaign for the Restoration of the Sir Casimir Gzowski Monument - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
2026.MM43.96.s:
The Sir Casimir Gzowski Monument was constructed in 1968 through a close collaboration between the Ontario Institute of Engineers, Toronto’s Polish community, and the City of Toronto. Situated in a City of Toronto park of the same name, this impressive memorial commemorates the life and work of Sir Casimir Gzowski (1813 – 1898), who was knighted by Queen Victoria in 1890 for his vast contributions to Ontario and Canada. The monument is an asset in the City's Public Art and Monuments Collection, managed by Economic Development and Culture.

The monument’s substantial structure, designed by architect Richard R. D’Wonnik, symbolizes the major facets of Sir Casimir Gzowski’s professional life; his work as an engineer, in the military, and as a statesman. Features such as railway tracks and I-beams atop the concrete tower allude to the bridges and railroads Sir Gzowski built across Ontario. The spike positioned on top of the monument is a beacon, which was intended to guide boats into the Toronto harbour at the time of construction.

The centrepiece of the monument is a bronze bust of Sir Casimir Gzowski, sculpted by Frederick A. Turner Dunbar. Turner Dunbar's design was selected by the Ontario Institute of Engineers, a fitting tribute as Sir Casimir Gzowski helped found the Engineer Institute of Canada during his time serving as a senator of the University of Toronto. The interior of the monument also features didactic panels, which share historic context and images of Sir Casimir Gzowski's life and legacy.

Since its installation, the Sir Casimir Gzowski Monument has undergone several restoration campaigns, including standard care and maintenance, repair of the railway ties, and replacement of the bronze bust after the original was stolen in the 1980s.

Now, more than half a century after its creation, the memorial requires comprehensive revitalization, including the rehabilitation of both structural and symbolic elements.

Since the beginning, professional engineers and Toronto's Polish community have served as essential partners in the realization and ongoing care of this unique monument. It is with the same spirit of stewardship that the Association of Polish Engineers in Canada established the Sir Casimir Gzowski Monument Revitalization Committee. Comprised of community volunteers, the Committee is dedicated to the preservation of the monument as a site of tribute and meaning for residents and visitors. The Committee has generously offered to spearhead a fundraising campaign to support the City of Toronto’s upcoming rehabilitation work, known as the Sir Casimir Gzowski Monument restoration project.

By leading a fundraising campaign for the Sir Casimir Gzowski Monument restoration project, the Committee’s efforts ensure that this significant structure continues to commemorate Sir Casimir Gzowski, the Polish Canadian community, and all that they have contributed to Toronto and beyond.

Reason for Urgency:

This motion is urgent to ensure that the Sir Casimir Gzowski Monument Revitalization Committee can begin fundraising for the restoration project.

2026.MM43.98.t: Authorizing Development Charge Refunds for Condominium Projects Converting to Purpose-built Rental Tenure - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Nick Mantas
2026.MM43.98.s:
Toronto Municipal Code Chapter 415, Development of Land, allows the City to recover additional development charges where a purpose-built rental development subsequently converts to condominium ownership. However, where a project that has already paid development charges converts from a condominium to purpose-built rental prior to occupancy, there is currently no authority to charge the corresponding rate and issue a refund.

Residential developments in the City of Toronto are subject to different development charge rates depending on tenure. Rental developments are eligible for statutory and discretionary discounts, with the discounted amount depending on the number of bedrooms in a unit.

Through Bill 17, residential development charges are now payable at occupancy. Where a project converts from condominium ownership to purpose-built rental before occupancy, the appropriate rental rate can be applied when development charges become payable. However, a limited number of projects paid development charges before occupancy under a previous legislative framework, or through an early payment, and later converted to purpose-built rental.

In these cases, the amount paid may exceed the amount that would have applied had the project been identified as purpose-built rental at the time of payment. This Motion authorizes the Chief Financial Officer and Treasurer to refund that difference, together with any corresponding interest adjustments, where a project converts to purpose-built rental prior to first partial occupancy, to reflect the appropriate rate. This Motion is also aligned with the City of Toronto’s goal to reduce barriers to developing new rental homes.

Reason for Urgency:

This is time sensitive to ensure Council approval to be able to proceed with refund(s) for applicable properties which have been converted from condominiums to purpose-built rentals.
2026.MM43.98.r:
Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Nick Mantas, recommends that:

1. City Council authorize the Chief Financial Officer and Treasurer, in the event development charges are paid early at the rates applicable to non-rental residential development and the units are later determined to be Purpose Built Rental prior to first partial occupancy, to refund the difference between the development charge amount paid and the development charge amount payable for Purpose Built Rental Units. The refund shall also include any corresponding adjustment to interest payable under the Development Charges Act, 1997 that would have applied had the dwelling unit or units qualified as Purpose Built Rental Units at the time the development charge was originally paid or payable.

2026.MM43.101.t: Assumption of Lighting Maintenance and Repair on Thomas Clark Way - by Councillor Shelley Carroll, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.101.s:
Thomas Clark Way was dedicated as a future public street more than a decade ago but remains unassumed because the City has not completed the road extension required to bring it into the municipal road network. While the adjacent developments have long since been completed and occupied, repeated delays to the City's construction schedule have left the roadway in administrative limbo, with no clear responsibility for essential public infrastructure.

In 2022, as part of IA38.1 and Answer IA38.1a on Status of Thomas Clark Way Extension, City staff advised that construction of the Thomas Clark Way extension was expected to begin in 2023 after work had been delayed during the COVID-19 pandemic. That timeline was subsequently pushed to August 2026, and the Councillors office has now been advised that construction has been delayed again until at least April 2027. As a result, the road remains unassumed years after development was completed.

For more than two years, three streetlights on Thomas Clark Way have been inoperable. Because the roadway has not been assumed, neither the City nor Toronto Hydro has accepted responsibility for maintaining the lighting, while the condominium corporation has been left responsible for infrastructure that would ordinarily form part of the public street network. Given that the prolonged delay in assuming the roadway is the result of repeated City delays rather than any action by the property owner, it is unreasonable to continue expecting the condominium corporation to bear responsibility for infrastructure that should already be part of the City's transportation network.

The absence of functioning streetlights creates an ongoing safety hazard for residents, pedestrians, and motorists. Until the roadway is assumed, the City should undertake the necessary repairs and maintenance of the streetlighting to protect public safety and ensure that residents are not disadvantaged by delays beyond their control.

Reason for Urgency:

This motion is urgent because City staff have recently advised that construction of the Thomas Clark Way road extension has been delayed until 2027, further postponing the assumption of the roadway and prolonging the uncertainty over responsibility for its streetlighting. As a result, residents will continue to be subjected to unsafe conditions caused by inoperable streetlights for an extended period unless immediate action is taken. Given that this is the last regular meeting of Council before the end of the term, deferring consideration would unnecessarily delay a solution to an ongoing public safety issue.
2026.MM43.101.r:
Councillor Shelley Carroll, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the General Manager, Transportation Services, through the Transportation Electrical Construction and Maintenance Group, in consultation with Toronto Hydro, to undertake the necessary repairs to the lighting on Thomas Clark Drive in advance of the full road assumption.

2026.MM43.103.t: Amending Item 2022.TE34.35 - 200 Queens Quay West - Zoning By-law Amendment - Final Report - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
2026.MM43.103.s:
At its meeting of July 19, 20, 21 and 22, 2022, City Council adopted Item TE34.35, approving a Zoning By-law Amendment Application at 200, 207, 208, 211, 218, 228 and 230 Queens Quay West and 8 York Street. Council’s approval permitted a 59-storey mixed use building at 200 Queens Quay West with 997 dwelling units, of which at least 76 and up to 79 were proposed as affordable rental dwelling units. The minimum requirement of at least 76 affordable rental dwelling units, with a 40 year affordability period, was secured as a community benefit in the site-specific Zoning By-law Amendment for the development (By-law 1012-2022), and at least 76 and up to 79 affordable rental dwelling units was then secured within the registered Section 37 Agreement (AT6891344). The affordable rental dwelling units were secured in accordance with terms that, among other matters, required that the minimum unit sizes of the affordable rental dwelling units be no less than the minimum and average sizes of the market units, and also set out specific minimum average unit sizes for the affordable housing units by unit type which are larger than the minimum average unit sizes of the market units by unit type.

Additionally, City Council approved the provision of financial incentives under the City’s Open Door program, for up to 79 affordable rental dwelling units including exemptions of fees for planning applications, building permits, parkland dedication and development charges, and exemptions from taxation for municipal and school purposes for the 40 year affordability period. City Council also authorized the Executive Director, Housing Secretariat to execute a municipal housing facility agreement (“Contribution Agreement”) with the owner for the development of the affordable housing units.

Since the Council decision, the development of the mixed-use building has advanced to site plan approval including the issuance of Notice of Approval Conditions and the issuance of a building permit. The mixed-use building is currently under construction and includes 974 dwelling units, of which 78 are affordable rental dwelling units. The owner has advised that they are proposing to reduce the specific minimum average sizes of the affordable rental dwelling units to align with the minimum average sizes of the market units by type, and to increase the number of affordable rental dwelling units to at least 82 and up to 90 units to address market demand.

As the site-specific zoning by-law requires at least 76 affordable rental dwelling units and requires specific minimum average unit sizes by unit type for the affordable rental dwelling units which exceed the average sizes of the market units by type, the owner is proposing to seek a minor variance from the Committee of Adjustment to i) reduce the specific minimum average sizes by unit type of the affordable rental dwelling units to align with the minimum average sizes by unit type of the market units; and ii) to increase the amount of affordable rental dwelling units from at least 76 to at least 82 affordable rental dwelling units. The more general By-law requirement that the minimum unit sizes of the affordable rental dwelling units be no less than the minimum and average sizes of the market units would be retained. Community Planning, City Planning and Housing Development Office staff have reviewed the proposed changes and are of the opinion that the proposed revisions are appropriate, as the affordable rental dwelling unit sizes would continue to be no less than the minimum and average sizes of the market units, and the provision of additional affordable rental dwelling units supports important City housing objectives.

If the Committee of Adjustment authorizes a minor variance to reduce the specific sizes of the affordable rental dwelling units and increase the minimum number of affordable rental dwelling units, an amendment to the existing Section 37 Agreement would be required. An amendment to the existing Contribution Agreement would also be required to extend the City incentives for a minimum of 82 and up to 90 affordable rental housing units to be affordable at 100 percent Average Market Rents under the Open Door program for a 40-year affordability period.

This motion is urgent as this building is currently under construction and any changes need to be made so it can stay on track.
