2026.MM43.104.t: Stopping Auto Theft Before It Starts: Requiring Stronger Anti-Theft Technologies in New Vehicles - by Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll
2026.MM43.104.s:
Auto theft remains a serious public safety concern in Toronto and across Canada, posing significant risks to residents, communities, and law enforcement while imposing substantial costs on vehicle owners, insurers, businesses, and governments. Far more than a property crime, auto theft fuels organized criminal activity, supports other illegal enterprises, places increasing demands on police resources, and creates dangerous situations during thefts, investigations, and vehicle recoveries.

Toronto Police Service data shows that auto theft remains a significant public safety challenge, despite meaningful progress achieved through targeted enforcement and coordinated action. In 2025, reported auto thefts declined by nearly 24 per cent compared to the previous year, reflecting the success of dedicated enforcement initiatives, intelligence-led investigations, and collaboration with policing and government partners. However, the Toronto Police Service has consistently emphasized that organized criminal networks continue to exploit vulnerabilities in vehicle security systems and that enforcement alone cannot fully address the problem. While police have made important gains in disrupting these criminal organizations, stronger preventative measures at the vehicle manufacturing stage are needed to reduce opportunities for theft before they occur.

As auto theft methods continue to evolve, stronger preventative measures are needed at the vehicle design and manufacturing stage. Criminals increasingly exploit vulnerabilities in electronic key systems, vehicle communications, and onboard technologies, enabling some vehicles to be stolen within minutes. Automobile manufacturers have a critical role to play by incorporating more effective anti-theft technologies into every new vehicle sold in Canada.

The Government of Canada should require automobile manufacturers to make enhanced anti-theft technologies standard equipment in all new vehicles, including improved immobilization systems, stronger encryption, more secure keyless entry systems, advanced authentication technologies, and other innovations that prevent unauthorized vehicle access and operation. Strengthening national vehicle security standards would complement police enforcement efforts, improve public safety, reduce opportunities for organized crime, better protect Canadian consumers, and help reduce the social and economic impacts of auto theft.

Reason for Urgency:

Seven thousand, four hundred and twenty-one (7,421) auto thefts occurred across Toronto in 2025 and we need to pursue every auto theft prevention measure possible.
2026.MM43.104.r:
Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll, recommends that:

1. City Council request the Government of Canada, through the Minister of Transport, to amend the Motor Vehicle Safety Regulations under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act to require that all new motor vehicles sold in Canada be equipped with enhanced anti-theft technologies as standard equipment, including improved immobilization systems, vehicle locating technology, stronger encryption, more secure keyless entry systems, advanced authentication technologies, and other vehicle security measures designed to prevent unauthorized access and theft.

2026.MM43.106.t: Facilitating Safe Construction Access for the Development at 8 to 10 Hyde Park Circle - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
2026.MM43.106.s:
Construction has begun on a development located at 8 to 10 Hyde Park Circle, properties with street addresses facing into a cul-de-sac and with rear and side frontages onto Post Road and Bayview Avenue. As approved, the development will eventually route vehicular access onto Post Road rather than into Hyde Park Circle, as Post Road has greater capacity to accommodate the traffic the project will generate. Similarly, throughout the approval process for this application the City, applicant and community have understood that access to the site during construction would be facilitated through Post Road.

As it stands, access to the site in early stages of construction has been routed through Hyde Park Circle due to a narrow reserve along the north side of Post Road, which must be addressed to facilitate access. This situation has resulted in significant concern for residents on Hyde Park Circle, whose dead-end street has been the sole access point for trucks and construction equipment coming in and out of the site. This has resulted in concerns about safety as trucks waiting to enter the site have blocked access into the area, compromising resident and emergency vehicle access.

A permanent solution to address this reserve is being worked out by the applicant and Corporate Real Estate Management, but an interim solution is needed to ensure that residents on Hyde Park Circle do not continue to bear the brunt of construction for the duration of this project.

Reason for Urgency:

This motion is urgent as construction is underway at 8 to 10 Hyde Park Circle and a solution must be advanced in order to facilitate access to the site off of Post Road and mitigate safety and access impacts for residents on Hyde Park Circle.
2026.MM43.106.r:
Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle, recommends that:

1. City Council request the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management, in consultation with the General Manager, Transportation Services, the Executive Director, Development Review, and the City Solicitor, to review on an expedited basis the ownership and legal status of the reserve situated between the lands municipally known as 8 to 10 Hyde Park Circle and Post Road, and to determine whether temporary construction access across the reserve may be authorized under existing delegated authority, subject to all necessary legal, title, engineering, traffic-safety, development-approval, insurance, financial-security, restoration and permitting requirements and terms satisfactory to the appropriate City officials.

2. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services, to continue addressing construction-related compliance and neighbourhood impacts on Hyde Park Circle through the applicable permit, inspection and enforcement processes while the temporary-access review is underway.

2026.MM43.107.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds from the development at 1478 to 1496 Kingston Road for a decorative Pedestrian Crossing at Kingston Road at Eastwood Avenue - by Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Jon Burnside
2026.MM43.107.s:
Royal Canadian Legion Scarboro Branch 13 has been a cornerstone of the Birch Cliff community for more than a century. Operating from the Scarboro Veterans Memorial Hall at 1577 Kingston Road, built in 1922 following the First World War, the Branch has provided generations of veterans, their families and local residents with a place of remembrance, fellowship and community service.

Reflecting strong advocacy from local residents, veterans, and community members, a new signalized pedestrian crossing at Kingston Road and Kildonan Drive/Eastwood Avenue in front of the Legion is currently being installed. This initiative, intended to improve safety for seniors, veterans, people with disabilities and other vulnerable road users, was successfully approved by Scarborough Community Council and City Council and is now moving toward implementation by this fall.

This motion would advance funds to decorate the new crosswalk, serving as a daily reminder of the courage and sacrifice of Canada’s veterans, establish a distinguished gateway to Branch 13 and strengthen the connection between Kingston Road’s future growth and the neighbourhood’s proud history. It is a modest investment with an enduring civic impact and strong community support would honour those who served while creating a safer, more welcoming and meaningful public realm for generations to come.

This matter is urgent because installation of the new signalized pedestrian crossing at Kingston Road and Eastwood Avenue/Kildonan Drive is proceeding, and City staff require timely direction to incorporate the proposed decorative design into the project. Providing direction at this stage will allow the decorative crossing to be coordinated with the scheduled installation, avoid potential delays or additional costs associated with completing the work separately, and create a lasting tribute near the Royal Canadian Legion Scarboro Branch 13 going into its 105 years of service to veterans and the Birch Cliff community.

2026.MM43.108.t: Exploring Alternative Governance Models for Biidaasige Park - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
2026.MM43.108.s:
Biidaasige Park is one of Toronto’s largest and most significant new parks and public spaces to open in a generation. Brought to life through the tri-government-funded Port Lands Flood Protection Project, its unique scale, design, ecological restoration, public art, and Indigenous placekeeping elements make it a landmark destination and an important piece of social infrastructure. The park will serve residents and visitors for generations while standing as a testament to Toronto’s commitment to Reconciliation, Indigenous stewardship, and creating world-class public spaces.

Given the scale of public investment, the deep engagement with multiple stakeholders and partners and the long-term importance of this asset, it is timely and appropriate to explore governance models that could enhance stewardship, programming, operations, and maintenance. Many leading cities have successfully complemented municipal park management through conservancies and other collaborative partnerships that help sustain iconic public spaces. This review would examine whether similar approaches could support the long-term success of Biidaasige Park while complementing the Waterfront Toronto-led, tri-government-funded Early Activation Strategy being implemented on the future Biidaasige Park North and adjacent lands, helping identify opportunities to strengthen programming, partnerships, and the enduring value of the park as the eastern waterfront continues to evolve.

Reason for Urgency:

This item is deemed urgent as there are no standing committees scheduled to advance this work in a timely way.
2026.MM43.108.r:
Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, recommends that:

1. City Council request the Deputy City Manager, Community and Emergency Services, in consultation with the Chief Executive Officer of Waterfront Toronto and in collaboration with the General Manager, Parks and Recreation, the General Manager, Economic Development, the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning and the City Solicitor to review precedents and best practices for alternative models of collaborative park governance in order to create a non-profit park conservancy model for the long-term stewardship and enhancement of Biidaasige Park concurrent with advancement of the tri-government funded Early Activation Strategy; and to facilitate engagement with key stakeholders, including the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority, Indigenous groups, the Lassonde Art Trail Foundation, and other relevant stakeholders; and report on the findings to the appropriate standing committee in the second half of 2027.

1. 2026.MM43.110.s:
The Jean Augustine Centre for Young Women's Empowerment is an important community organization that supports hundreds of girls and young women through mentorship, education, leadership development, and wraparound supports.

The Centre's current lease in Etobicoke–Lakeshore is coming to an end, creating uncertainty about its future location, it is important to explore opportunities to secure a long-term home.

This is a proactive step to preserve an invaluable community asset, strengthen access to local programming, and ensure that organizations delivering critical services to residents have a stable, affordable home for years to come.

Reason for Urgency:

The Centre's current lease in Etobicoke–Lakeshore is coming to an end.
2026.MM43.110.r:
Councillor Amber Morley, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, recommends that:

1. City Council request the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management and the Executive Director, Social Development, in consultation with the Toronto District School Board, and other relevant divisions and agencies, to explore the feasibility of transitioning 300 Birmingham Street at the end of the current lease term into a Community Hub under the Community Space Tenancy Policy, and report back to the Economic and Community Development Committee in the second quarter of 2027.

2. City Council request the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management and the Executive Director, Social Development to consider Jean Augustine Centre and other eligible non-profit service providers as co-located below-market tenants under the Community Space Tenancy Policy at 300 Birmingham Street.

m.x:
City Council on July 29 and 30, 2026, adopted the following:

2. City Council request the Executive Director, Corporate Real Estate Management and the Executive Director, Social Development to consider Jean Augustine Centre and other eligible non-profit service providers as co-located below-market tenants under the Community Space Tenancy Policy at 300 Birmingham Street.

2026.MM43.111.t: 340 St Clements Avenue - Request for City Solicitor to Attend at the Toronto Local Appeal Body - by Councillor Mike Colle, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.111.s:
In June 2026, the applicant applied to the Committee of Adjustment for variances to the City-wide Zoning By-law 569-2013 in order to allow the construction of a six-storey apartment building, containing 54 dwelling units (the “Application”).

The applicant sought eleven variances relating to the maximum permitted building length, minimum front, rear and side yard setbacks, minimum landscaping area, minimum drive aisle width, parking space dimensions, visitor parking requirements, loading space requirements, and minimum bicycle parking access aisle width.

In its report dated July 6, 2026, City Planning Staff recommended that the Committee of Adjustment defer the Application. City Planning Staff sought further discussions with the applicant to improve the proposed built form and requested that the Committee of Adjustment defer this Application until the next scheduled meeting (the Staff Report is attached as Attachment 1).

On July 9, 2026, the North York District Panel of the Committee of Adjustment refused the Application. A copy of the Decision of the Committee of Adjustment is attached as Attachment 2.

The applicant has appealed the refusal to the Toronto Local Appeal Body (the “Appeal”) through their Notice of Appeal dated July 29, 2026. A copy of the Notice of Appeal is attached as Attachment 3.

This motion will authorize and direct the City Solicitor to attend the Toronto Local Appeal Body, along with appropriate City staff and any external consultants retained as necessary, in order to oppose the Appeal.

This Motion will also authorize the City Solicitor to resolve the matter on behalf of the City in her discretion. This motion is time sensitive and urgent as the City Solicitor requires instructions to obtain party status in the Appeal and subsequently attend the hearing in opposition to the Appeal.
2026.MM43.111.r:
Councillor Mike Colle, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the City Solicitor to seek party status at the Toronto Local Appeal Body, and to attend the Toronto Local Appeal Body hearing, with appropriate City staff, in order to support the Committee of Adjustment’s decision to refuse Application A0208/26NY, respecting 340 St Clements Avenue.

2. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to retain outside consultants as necessary.

3. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to negotiate a resolution regarding 340 St Clements Avenue (Application A0208/26NY) and authorize the City Solicitor to resolve the matter on behalf of the City, at their discretion, after consultation with the Ward Councillor and the Director of Community Planning, North York District.

2. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to retain outside consultants as necessary.

3. 2026.MM43.112.t: 39 Norfield Crescent - Request for City Solicitor to Attend at the Toronto Local Appeal Body - by Councillor Vincent Crisanti, seconded by Councillor Stephen Holyday
2026.MM43.112.s:
This Motion will give the City Solicitor authority to appeal the Committee of Adjustment’s decision approving the minor variance application at 39 Norfield Crescent (A0178/26EYK); to attend the Toronto Local Appeal Body to oppose the development proposed in application A0178/26EYK; to retain outside consultants as necessary; and to negotiate a settlement of the appeal.

The Applicant applied to the Committee of Adjustment to request a variance from City-wide Zoning By-law 569-2013 (Application A0178/26EYK) to construct a second storey addition above the existing dwelling and to maintain the existing one-storey east side addition (the “Application”). The altered dwelling would contain a total of four units. To facilitate the Application, a variance for front yard setback is required.

On July 16, 2026, the Committee of Adjustment approved the Application (the “Decision”). A copy of the Decision is attached as Attachment 1.

In order for the City to continue to effectively assess and call its case, the City Solicitor requires the expertise of an external consultant to advise on the Applicant’s proposed plan, and to potentially make recommendations respecting a solution.

To preserve the City’s right of appeal, the City Solicitor filed an appeal of the Committee of Adjustment’s decision with the Toronto Local Appeal Body on July 27, 2026.

This matter is time-sensitive and urgent, as the appeal has already been filed to safeguard the City’s statutory rights.

Reason for Urgency:

If the City does not obtain Council authority and file an appeal within the applicable appeal period, the Committee of Adjustment approval will stand, and the City will lose its right to appeal to the Toronto Local Appeal Body. As a result, the matter can not wait until a later Council meeting.
2026.MM43.112.r:
Councillor Vincent Crisanti, seconded by Councillor Stephen Holyday, recommends that:

1. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to appeal the Committee of Adjustment’s decision regarding 39 Norfield Crescent (Application A0178/26EYK) and to attend the Toronto Local Appeal Body to oppose the development proposed in Application A0178/26EYK.

2. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to retain outside consultants as necessary.

3. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to negotiate a settlement of the appeal and to resolve the matter on behalf of the City, in her discretion, after consulting with the Ward Councillor and the Director of Community Planning, Etobicoke York District.

2026.MM43.113.t: Amending 2022.EY30.2 - 340 Mill Road - Zoning By-law Amendment Application - Final Report to provide for a Development Charge Credit for cycling infrastructure requested by City Staff - by Councillor Stephen Holyday, seconded by Councillor Vincent Crisanti
2026.MM43.113.s:
he Applicant applied for an amendment to the former City of Etobicoke Zoning Code and the City-wide Zoning By-law 569-2013 for the property at 340 Mill Road (the "Site") to permit a 19-storey infill rental apartment building (the "Application"). It was approved by City Council at its meeting on March 9, 2022, through Item 2022.EY30.2 and will contain 191 rental dwelling units. The Application provides for much needed rental housing and secures improvements to the public realm.

The Application secured a Section 37 benefit as follows:

Prior to the issuance of the first above-grade building permit for the Site, the owner shall make a cash contribution to the City in the amount of one million and five hundred thousand dollars ($1,500,000), payable to the Treasurer, City of Toronto, for the provision of parkland improvements at Centennial Park and/or the provision of connecting cycling infrastructure along Burnhamthorpe Road from Etobicoke Creek to Mill Road, to the satisfaction of the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning and the General Manager of Parks, Forestry and Recreation, in consultation with the Ward Councillor;

The Applicant paid the Section 37 Cash Contribution on May 7, 2025.

The Multi-Use Trail works contemplated by this motion are separate from and in addition to the community benefits secured through the Section 37 Agreement. The Section 37 cash contribution has been paid in full and is intended to be allocated to parkland improvements at Centennial Park. No portion of the development charge credit shall be attributable to works funded or required through the Section 37 Agreement.

Following payment of same, City staff requested that the Applicant complete works on their site, through the development review process, to deliver a portion of a Multi-Use Trail on Burnhamthorpe between the Mississauga border and Mill Road. The Multi-Use Trail is intended to close a key gap in the active transportation network contemplated by the 2025 – 2027 Cycling Program. Specifically, it will provide a safe, accessible connection between the existing Multi-Use Trail on Burnhamthorpe Road, which links to the trail system on the west side of the Mississauga border, with the recently installed bi-directional cycle track on Mill Road, the recently installed Multi-Use Trail on Centennial Park Boulevard, as well as the future cycling infrastructure on Rathburn Road.

Given that the proposed Multi-Use Trail works are separate from the Section 37 community benefit contribution and implement a City cycling infrastructure project, the most efficient avenue to allow for compensation of the Applicant’s works set out above is to provide for a development charge credit against the road component of the Applicant’s development charge. The total estimated cost of the works is $95,358.

City staff are supportive of the motion, as set out in Attachment 1.

Reason for Urgency:

The motion is urgent because it amends the funding framework for enabling cycling infrastructure and allows the developer to proceed with providing an important connection in the Multi-Use Trail on Burnhamthorpe between the Mississauga border and Mill Road implementing the objectives of the City's overall cycling plan.
2026.MM43.113.r:
Councillor Stephen Holyday, seconded by Councillor Vincent Crisanti, recommends that:

1. City Council amend its decision on item 2022.EY30.2 by adding the following recommendations:

7. City Council approve a development charge credit against the Road component of the Development Charges for the design and construction by the Owner of the Multi-Use Trail on Burnhamthorpe between the Mississauga border and Mill Road to the satisfaction of the Executive Director, Development Review, in consultation with the General Manager Transportation Services. The development charge credit shall be in an amount that is the lesser of the cost incurred by the Owner of designing and constructing the Multi-Use Trail, as approved by the Executive Director, Development Review in consultation with the General Manager Transportation Services, and the Road component of development charges payable for the development in accordance with the City's Development Charges By-law, as may be amended from time to time.

2026.MM43.114.t: Malvern Area Community Facilities and Services Working Group - Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Neethan Shan
2026.MM43.114.s:
The proposed developments in the Malvern area, including the Malvern Town Centre, represent a significant opportunity to reshape the community to support major commercial and civic destinations in Scarborough North. Considerations to support new residents and jobs in the Malvern area and how development is phased over time include important matters such as housing, transportation (including new pedestrian and cycling connections), new parks and open spaces, the public realm, and the delivery of community services in Malvern and surrounding neighbourhoods.

Malvern is home to a large and diverse population, including significant Black, Indigenous and newcomer communities, as well as seniors, youth and other equity-deserving groups. The needs and experiences of these communities should help inform the planning of community facilities and services associated with the redevelopment.

Malvern is also served by long-standing community anchor organizations with deep local relationships and extensive experience addressing health, social-service, cultural and community-infrastructure priorities across Black, Indigenous and other communities.

Through the Toronto Poverty Reduction Strategy, the Toronto Action Plan to Confront Anti-Black Racism and other Council-approved equity frameworks, the City has committed to ensuring that major planning and development processes respond to communities facing systemic barriers and produce equitable community outcomes.

To support a coordinated effort for broader collaboration between members of the Malvern community and development proponents, a structured forum is needed to bring together community organizations, residents, service providers, development stakeholders and appropriate City divisions. This forum would support sustained coordination, identify community priorities, address service continuity, and ensure that the needs of community-service providers and users remain part of the City’s ongoing planning and implementation work.

Reason for Urgency:

The urgency is that a settlement had been reached between the City and the Appellant and will be voted on at this Council meeting (CC43.23). Once the settlement is approved by this Council meeting it is vital that continuing community engagement about the project continue during the election period.
2026.MM43.114.r:
Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Neethan Shan, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the Executive Director, Development Review, in consultation with the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, the Executive Director, Social Development, the General Manager, Economic Development, and other appropriate City officials, to convene a Malvern Area Community Facilities and Services Working Group as part of community consultations for Planning Act applications as stipulated by the Official Plan:

a. comprising representatives from the local community including, the TAIBU Community Health Centre, Native Child and Family Services of Toronto, MyMalvern, local residents and community-service users, other relevant community organizations, local City Councillors, and appropriate City divisions and agencies, with the owner or applicant of development(s) in the Malvern area being invited to participate as appropriate to the stage of the planning and development process;

b. providing a forum for the Working Group members to identify local priorities and inform the City’s ongoing work respecting community facilities and services associated with the development in the Malvern area, with particular attention to service continuity, redevelopment phasing, the operational and accessibility needs of community-service providers that coordinates with the City, community organizations, residents and such service providers; and

c. establishing a terms of reference and identify any resourcing requirements, in consultation with Working Group members, with the first meeting to be convened by the end of the first quarter of 2027, and a report from the Executive Director, Development Review to the appropriate Committee by the end of the second quarter of 2027 on the Working Group’s establishment, priorities and work, including any additional authorities or resources required.

2026.MM43.116.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for Locally Branded Street Signs for the Bedford Park Neighbourhood - by Councillor Mike Colle, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.116.s:
Bedford Park is one of Toronto's oldest established neighbourhoods, with origins dating back to the late 19th century. Initially a rural farming hamlet and popular stop for farmers travelling along Yonge Street to markets in downtown Toronto, the community grew rapidly following the arrival of the Metropolitan Street Railway in 1890, which spurred residential development and helped shape the neighbourhood that exists today. The area is widely believed to have taken its name from the Bedford Park Hotel, which opened in 1873 and became a prominent local landmark, with the name later extending to the surrounding community and post office.

Today, Bedford Park remains a well-recognized historic neighbourhood whose identity has endured for more than 150 years. The neighbourhood's name is reflected in local institutions, including Bedford Park Public School, and continues to be widely used by residents, businesses, and community organizations.

Installing neighbourhood street signage featuring the Bedford Park moniker would reinforce the area's long-standing identity, celebrate its historical significance, and strengthen neighbourhood wayfinding and community pride for residents and visitors alike.

The reason for urgency is that local Residents Association has been hard at work collaborating with the Councillor’s office for an extended period of time on various public realm projects and this initiative became the preferred project to seek approval in time for Bedford Park Residents Organization to celebrate a milestone anniversary this year and this is the last meeting of Council of this term to provide approval.

1. City Council increase the 2026-2035 Capital Budget and Plan for Transportation Services by $37,596.72 gross, $0 debt, fully funded by Section 37 community benefits obtained from the development at 1580 Avenue Road (Source Account: XR3026-3701016), to be utilized to fabricate and install street signage recognizing the Bedford Park neighbourhood at 161 locations - Lawrence Avenue West, Jedburgh Road, Elm Road and Greer Road (Signs and Markings Asset Management, CTP726-08).

2026.MM43.117.t: Authorization to Release Section 42 Funds for a Refresh and a Water Feature for Coxwell Common - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata
2026.MM43.117.s:
After 30 years, the green space at 1555 Danforth at Coxwell officially became a city park. It is now formally a park with an official name - Coxwell Common. For all these years it has been a beautiful respite and community gathering space along the busy Danforth. It also hosts the Courtyard Farmers’ Market each week.

Unlike most other green spaces, it was built with a full irrigation system that leads to a circle in the middle of the park which was to be a water feature. Since the beginning the circle has

only ever had a tree with some plantings.

A water feature would improve the overall enjoyment of the park as one of only of two green spaces on the Danforth between Broadview and Victoria Park.

The planting beds would benefit from renewal and additional planting to improve biodiversity, visual appeal, climate resilience, and overall park quality.

Now that it is formally parks property, funds can be allocated to review all of the below ground water infrastructure and the feasibility and design of a water feature. Funds are available to support local park and recreation improvements that provide broad community benefits.

Reason for urgency:

The community has been waiting for improvements at this site for some time. As funds have been identified it is time to advance this work without delay.

2026.MM43.118.t: Revitalizing St. Patrick’s Market Square - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
2026.MM43.118.s:
The City of Toronto is developing a long-term real estate strategy for the Grange Precinct in downtown Toronto. This work is led by CreateTO on behalf of the City and in close collaboration with community partners. The precinct includes several important public assets, including St. Patrick's Market, St. Patrick's Market Square, Harrison Pool, University Settlement, and Grange Park.

The Grange Precinct is a vital part of Toronto's downtown west community. It is home to significant cultural institutions, community-serving organizations, public spaces, and a diverse population of residents. The area serves as an important gathering place, connecting neighbourhoods while supporting recreation, culture, social services, and community programming.

The Grange Precinct Real Estate Strategy seeks to establish a long-term vision for the area by:

a. coordinating capital investments across City divisions and agencies;

b. maximizing the public value and benefit of City-owned assets;

c. responding to community social, recreational, and programmatic needs; and

d. improving accessibility, connectivity, and the quality of the public realm throughout the precinct.

This work is being informed through a cross-divisional planning process and community engagement. Community consultation has consistently identified the importance of St. Patrick's Market Square parkette as a valued public space and gathering place. Residents and stakeholders have also expressed interest in seeing improvements delivered as early as possible while longer-term planning for the precinct continues.

This motion would support the exploration of opportunities to advance near-term improvements to St. Patrick's Market Square parkette through a phased approach that complements the broader Grange Precinct Real Estate Strategy. It would also ensure that potential enhancements identified by the community, including outdoor fitness equipment and other recreational amenities, are considered through future public consultation and design work.

Reason for Urgency:

The Grange Precinct Real Estate Strategy is currently underway and, separately, planning for future park capital investments is being considered through the City's upcoming budget processes. This motion is therefore urgent to provide direction to staff to evaluate opportunities for advancing improvements to St. Patrick's Market Square and to ensure that community priorities are considered as work on the broader precinct strategy proceeds.
2026.MM43.118.r:
Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise, recommends that:

1. City Council request the General Manager, Parks and Recreation, in consultation with the Chief Executive Officer, CreateTO, to review opportunities to expedite the phased delivery of improvements to St. Patrick's Market Square parkette as part of the City's broader Grange Precinct Real Estate Strategy and to include potential enhancements identified through community feedback, including outdoor fitness equipment and other recreational amenities, as part of future public consultations and design considerations.

2026.MM43.119.t: Considering the Cumulative Impacts of Development Activity in Cliffcrest to Ensure Proper Planning and Balanced Growth - by Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
2026.MM43.119.s:
In recent years, an unprecedented number of development applications have been considered or approved for medium-to-large-scale residential buildings in the Cliffcrest neighbourhood, along Kingston Road generally between Brimley Road and Markham Road. The increase in housing supply and options is welcome as Toronto continues to address a housing affordability crisis.

The Cliffcrest neighbourhood is uniquely situated along the top of the Scarborough Bluffs, where outstanding natural beauty and environmental sensitivity intersect with an established residential neighbourhood characterized by lower-intensity built form. The area also functions as an important gateway to the waterfront and adjacent parkland, making thoughtful long-term planning particularly important as redevelopment occurs.

This motion seeks to ensure that the attributes of the community are being considered alongside the review and approval of development applications, and that municipal and social services, environmental planning and protection, transportation infrastructure, public realm improvements, and local business activity are informed by the cumulative impacts of changes in built form along this stretch of Kingston Road. Better coordination between City divisions will support proactive service planning, infrastructure investment, and environmental stewardship as the neighbourhood evolves.

Establishing an ongoing process to monitor development activity and share information across relevant City divisions will help identify emerging trends early, support evidence-based decision-making, and ensure municipal planning responds proactively to neighbourhood change. The recommendation does not alter the planning approval process for individual applications, but instead seeks to improve coordination and long-term planning across City programs and services.

Reason for Urgency:

This matter is considered urgent because development applications continue to be submitted and advanced within the study area. Establishing coordinated monitoring now will allow City divisions and agencies to incorporate development activity into ongoing infrastructure, service, and environmental planning before cumulative impacts become more difficult and costly to address.
2026.MM43.119.r:
Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow, recommneds that:

1. City Council direct the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning to monitor development applications along Kingston Road generally between Brimley Road and Markham Road, and provide development activity findings to partner divisions and agencies involved in the review of municipal infrastructure, transportation, environment and public realm, community services and local business activity to assist in their long-term planning.

2026.MM43.120.t: Authorization to Release Section 45 Funds from the Development at 2328 to 2350 Kingston Road for a Public Art Mural - by Councilor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
2026.MM43.120.s:

This matter is considered urgent given the community’s desire for a replacement mural in the Cliffside neighbourhood following the demolition of longstanding murals in the area, and the developer’s willingness to partner with the City and community to create this public contribution in the near-term.

2026.MM43.121.t: Protecting Toronto’s Live Music Venues - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
2026.MM43.121.s:
Toronto’s live music scene is a cultural engine that has produced local and international stars. While the city boasts a vibrant collection of small and large venues, serving diverse communities, it is also facing major threats including rising rents and insurance and development pressures. Over the past few years, we’ve lost many live music venues in the City of Toronto and many others have been at risk, most recently Sneaky Dee’s.

Many divisions at the City of Toronto have been looking at what is possible to support live music venues to continue to thrive. This motion will enable staff to continue this work, reporting back as part of our Culture Connects plan.

This motion is urgent to enable staff to begin work to meet the report back timelines.
2026.MM43.121.r:
Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, recommends that:

1. City Council request the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, the General Manager, Economic Development and Culture, and the Interim Executive Director, Development Review, and any other divisions as needed, to continue efforts to address the current precarious state of live music venues, by taking proactive steps to protect existing venues and encourage establishment of new venues, such potential steps including but not be limited to: updating the Official Plan and Zoning By-laws; drafting design guidelines for mixed-use developments; exploring cultural heritage designations and land trusts; aligning with the Culture Connects and Sidewalks to Skylines action plans; consulting with industry stakeholders, venue operators and audiences; and other measures as required to support live music venues, reporting back as part of the Culture Connects report in 2027.

m.x:
City Council on July 29 and 30, 2026, adopted the following:

1. City Council request the Chief Planner and Executive Director, City Planning, the General Manager, Economic Development and Culture, and the Interim Executive Director, Development Review, and any other divisions as needed, to continue efforts to address the current precarious state of live music venues, by taking proactive steps to protect existing venues and encourage establishment of new venues, such potential steps including but not be limited to: updating the Official Plan and Zoning By-laws; drafting design guidelines for mixed-use developments; exploring cultural heritage designations and land trusts; aligning with the Culture Connects and Sidewalks to Skylines action plans; consulting with industry stakeholders, venue operators and audiences; and other measures as required to support live music venues, reporting back as part of the Culture Connects report in 2027.

2026.MM43.122.s:
Following further review and community consultation, accepting a cash contribution in lieu of the construction of the below-grade connection to Dufferin Station represents the best outcome for the community.

This motion directs the City to proceed with the cash contribution option, allowing the value which would otherwise have been allocated to the tunnel's construction to be redirected toward high-priority affordable housing initiatives, community and cultural amenities, and public realm improvements for Dufferin Subway Station identified through consultation with residents and stakeholders. This approach ensures that community benefits associated with the development are delivered in a manner that maximizes public value in a way that is responsive to current local needs.

2026.MM43.123.t: 74 Kirknewton Road - Request for City Solicitor to Attend at the Toronto Local Appeal Body - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
2026.MM43.123.s:
The Applicant applied to the Committee of Adjustment to request eight (8) variances from City-wide Zoning By-law 569-2013 (Application A0435/26TEY) to construct a new three-storey detached dwelling with front stairs to access the ground level; and to construct a new rear two-storey detached ancillary building containing one garden suite (the “Application”). Prior to the Committee of Adjustment hearing, two of the variances for the garden suite were removed from the Application and the variances were reduced to six (6), including building height, front yard setback and side yard setback for the main dwelling; rear yard setback and side yard setback for the garden suite; and rear yard soft landscaping.

On July 22, 2026, the Toronto and East York District Panel of the Committee of Adjustment approved the Application (the “Decision”). A copy of the Decision Notice is attached as Attachment 1. The last date of appeal is August 11, 2026.

For the City to continue to effectively assess its case, the City Solicitor requires the expertise of an external consultant to advise on the Applicant’s proposed plan, and to potentially make recommendations respecting a solution.

This Motion will authorize the City Solicitor to appeal the Decision to the Toronto Local Appeal Body and to resolve the matter on behalf of the City in their discretion.

This matter is time-sensitive and urgent as the last date of appeal is August 11, 2026.
2026.MM43.123.r:
Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconeded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, recommend that:

1. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to appeal the Committee of Adjustment’s approval of the Application A0435/26TEY in respect of the property municipally known as 74 Kirknewton Road (the “Appeal”) and to attend the Toronto Local Appeal Body hearing.

2. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to retain outside consultants as necessary.

3. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to resolve the Appeal and settle the matter on behalf of the City at their discretion in consultation with the Ward Councillor and the Director of Community Planning, Toronto and East York District.

2026.MM43.124.t: Provision of Access to Waste Receptacles On-Site for Customer Use in Quick-Serve Restaurants - by Councillor Michael Thompson, seconded by Councillor Neethan Shan
2026.MM43.124.s:
Some quick-serve restaurants do not provide their customers with access to on-site waste receptacles (i.e. garbage, recycling, organics) to dispose of waste after consuming food and drinks. Rather, in these establishments that do not have customer accessible waste receptacles, customers are left with no option other than to dispose of their waste in public space waste receptacles.

Public space waste receptacles, such as street litter bins, are not designed nor intended to accept materials generated from food service establishments in lieu of the establishment providing on-site waste receptacles. Council direction is required for Solid Waste Management Services staff to research available regulatory, licensing, operational, and legal mechanisms that could be implemented to require all food service establishments to provide on-site waste receptacles for use by their customers.

Reason for Urgency:

As Council is not scheduled to meet for the balance of the year, staff are requested to begin this work as soon as possible. This allows sufficient time over the summer to prepare and bring forward the appropriate recommendations.
2026.MM43.124.r:
Councillor Michael Thompson, seconded by Councillor Neethan Shan, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the General Manager, Solid Waste Management Services to work with appropriate City Divisions to take the necessary steps to mandate quick-serve restaurants to provide on-site waste receptacles for use by their customers, and report back to City Council if required.

m.x:
City Council on July 29 and 30, 2026, adopted the following:

1. City Council direct the General Manager, Solid Waste Management Services to work with appropriate City Divisions to take the necessary steps to mandate quick-serve restaurants to provide on-site waste receptacles for use by their customers, and report back to City Council if required.

2026.MM43.125.t: Dedicated Commercial Loading Zone at 623 Danforth Avenue - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata
2026.MM43.125.s:
With the installation of the Danforth Cycle Track in 2021, the commercial loading zone located adjacent to Pape Market Foodland at 623 Danforth Avenue was established to support the operational needs of the grocery local delivery business and was funded by Pape Market Food Land.

Another dedicated loading zone was also established adjacent to the Danforth Music Hall with the installation of a Motor Coach only zone to provide parking for the buses required for the business aspects related to performances at the venue.

Pape Market Foodland relies on regular and timely deliveries throughout the day to maintain its operations and serve the surrounding community.

Despite funding the Commercial Loading Zone, the business has experienced repeated parking enforcement penalties for delivery vehicles in while in the loading zone.

Providing Pape Market Foodland with exclusive use of the commercial loading zone would improve the efficiency of business operations, reduce conflicts over the use of the loading zone, and better support the continued operation of this longstanding local business. It would also live up to the city’s permission for this loading zone when the Cycle Track was installed on the Danforth.

Reason for Urgency:

This request is time-sensitive because Pape Market Foodland depends on frequent deliveries throughout the day, and continued competition for the loading zone, coupled with repeated enforcement penalties, is creating significant operational inefficiencies. Prompt action to provide exclusive access would help prevent further disruptions to the business and ensure uninterrupted service to the community that relies on it.
2026.MM43.125.r:
Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata, recommneds that:

1. City Council direct the General Manager, Transportation Services, to designate the existing commercial loading zone adjacent to Pape Market Foodland, 623 Danforth Avenue, for the exclusive use of the business and designate the zone with the appropriate signage.

2026.MM43.127.t: Consideration of Cycling Infrastructure Opportunities within the area of the Doris Avenue Road Extension Project south of Sheppard Avenue East - by Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe
2026.MM43.127.s:
The City of Toronto is advancing the City Council-approved interim offset intersection for the Doris Avenue Extension. This is a new road connection that will extend Tradewind Avenue north to Sheppard Avenue East. The project supports planned growth, improves local connectivity and enhances road safety and access for all road users, while creating a more attractive and comfortable streetscape.

In 2022, the City completed the North York Centre South Service Road Municipal Class Environmental Assessment Addendum, which evaluated options and proposed changes to Doris Avenue, Bonnington Place and Tradewind Avenue.

As a result of the evaluation undertaken, the study update recommended delivering the project in two phases, including a new road connection between Doris Avenue and Tradewind Avenue:

a. interim offset intersection: Designed to align with current development timing, and

b. ultimate realigned intersection: to be implemented in the future, subject to funding and land acquisition.

Both phases protect space for a future four‑lane road south of Sheppard Avenue East, with sidewalks on both sides and wider boulevards where possible.

The Doris Extension project will include the installation of bikeways along Sheppard Avenue East, between Kenneth Avenue and Yonge Street. While not part of the 2022 Environmental Assessment Addendum recommendations, they were subsequently assessed and identified as an important part of the cycling network.

Reason for Urgency:

The Doris Avenue Extension project is advancing through design and implementation stages, and timely consideration of cycling infrastructure opportunities is needed to ensure active transportation connections are incorporated before key design decisions are finalized. Early direction will allow Transportation Services to evaluate potential bikeway improvements as part of the project delivery process and avoid missing opportunities to create a safe and connected cycling network for the Avondale community.
2026.MM43.127.r:
Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe, recommends that:

1. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services, to review opportunities to create cycling facilities and bikeway improvements to connect the Avondale community with the existing and planned bikeways along Sheppard Avenue East and the overall cycling network, consistent with the City's Complete Streets Guidelines and Cycling Network Plan.

This motion also seeks authorization to waive any provisions that may be contained in a City policy, procedure, or guideline, that would otherwise restrict or delay a commemorative naming in honour of Howard Moscoe.

2026.MM43.130.t: Ensuring High Standard Ice Quality at City of Toronto’s Outdoor Artificial Outdoor Stand-Alone Pleasure Skating Facilities - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata
2026.MM43.130.s:
Outdoor artificial ice rinks are a vital recreational amenity that provide affordable access to physical activity, community gathering spaces, and winter recreation for residents of all ages

Every year the city is adding more skate trails which are open for pleasure skating only and at times draw many skaters over many hours.

There are no permits for skate trails. Without a permit system at times, it becomes difficult for the staff to control the actions of skaters as there is no penalty for poor behaviour.

Residents have expressed concerns regarding inconsistent quality at stand-alone pleasure outdoor skating trails due to a number of factors that are not present at Artificial Ice Rinks with boards.

While climate change is contributing to more frequent winter temperature fluctuations and freeze-thaw cycles that can negatively affect rink conditions there are steps that may can be taken to ensure the same level of ice quality on outdoor skate trails as rinks with boards.

Reason for Urgency:

A timely review will facilitate improvements which can be implemented in the new season.
2026.MM43.130.r:
Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the General Manager, Parks and Recreation to:

a. undertake a review of outdoor skate trail operations and maintenance practices with the objective of setting a standard for trails and improving and maintaining consistent, high-quality ice conditions, which can include more frequent flooding, scrapping and inspections;

b. review the current staffing model for skate trails for the upcoming winter season within the current budget to ensure a senior staff person is present and available to assist rink guards in dealing with prohibited activities; and

c. bring forward any resulting financial impacts for consideration in advance of the 2027 budget process.

2026.MM43.131.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 and Section 42 Funds for Improvements to Thompson Dog Off-Leash Area - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata
2026.MM43.131.s:
The Thompson Parkette Dog Off-Leash Area was established with the conversion of a local parkette to a Dog Off-Leash Area in order to meet the demands of rapid development in Riverside. It was also established to ensure that dog owners in Riverside had a standalone Dog Off-Leash Arearather than using the new Joel Weeks Park established with the Toronto Community Housing revitalization of Don Mount Court into Rivertowne.

The existing pea gravel surfacing has generated concerns regarding accessibility as well as maintenance, cleanliness, drainage, user comfort, and the tracking of gravel beyond the boundaries of the off-leash area.

Artificial turf has been successfully used in dog off-leash areas and recreational facilities to improve surface durability, accessibility, user experience, and year-round usability;

Parks currently has improvements planned to Thompson Off Leash by replacing the pea gravel. Artificial turf would enhance the functionality and enjoyment of the Dog Off-Leash Area for residents with an appropriate artificial turf surface designed for dog off-leash use and ensures user accessibility.

This option has much support in the community who have been awaiting an off leash at Riverside Square which has dedicated funds and has been delayed 10 years due to continued work on Richmond and Adelaide bridges and now the Ontario Line at East Harbour

There are sufficient storm sewers immediately adjacent to the Dog Off-Leash Area to provide for irrigation.

Reason for urgency: The current parks plan is to start to replace the pea gravel with wood chips however sufficient increased funding is available to change it over to accessible artificial turf.
2026.MM43.131.r:
Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata, recommends that:

1. City Council amend the 2026 to 2035 Capital Budget and Plan for Parks and Recreation by increasing the existing budget for the Thompson Parkette Off-Leash Area improvements by $646,569.72 gross and $0 debt, to be added to the existing approved project budget of $400,000, resulting in a revised total project budget of $1,046,569.72 gross and $0 debt, for design, installation, drainage improvements, site preparation, artificial turf conversion, and related works to enhance the Thompson Parkette Off-Leash Area, with the additional funding comprised of $300,000 gross and $0 debt in 2026 from Section 42 Above 5 percent Cash-in-lieu funds from Source Account XR2213-4201084 and $346,569.72 gross and $0 debt in 2027 from Section 37 funds from Source Account XR3026-3700880 for the purpose of a dog off-leash area in the ward.

2026.MM43.132.t: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds from the Development at 1478 to 1496 Kingston Road for a New Public Mural in Birchcliff Village - by Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
2026.MM43.132.s:
Birch Cliff Village, one of the earliest established villages in Scarborough, has a longstanding legacy of community identity and local entrepreneurship. Kingston Road, between Warden Avenue and Birchmount Road, continues to function as the central spine of the area, characterized by a mix of historic buildings, established institutions, and independent businesses. This corridor remains a vital destination for residents and visitors alike, supported by a diverse commercial base and ongoing development that signals continued growth and evolution.

The local community and business stakeholders have advocated for a public mural to help create a sense of arrival and identify. More recently, community members, including local artists and businesses near Birchcliff Avenue and Kingston Road, including Bodega by City Cottage, have advocated and volunteered their energy and resources to bring this longstanding idea forward. I am pleased to bring this forward to help support the continued renewal and investment in this community, so that it can be enjoyed by residents and visitors alike.

Reason for Urgency: This motion is considered urgent given ongoing beautification and renewal efforts by the community and local businesses.
2026.MM43.132.r:
Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow, recommends that:

2026.MM43.133.t: Amending Item 2025.TE19.9 - 90 Eastdale Avenue and 2 Secord Avenue - Zoning By-law Amendment Application - by Councillor Brad Bradford, seconded by Councillor James Pasternak
2026.MM43.133.s:
The purpose of this motion is to request City Council amend its previous decision on Item TE19.9 to add recommendations to facilitate the delegated payment-in-lieu of bike parking program process, including associated revisions to the draft Zoning By-law Amendment.

On February 5, 2025, City Council adopted as amended the Zoning By-law Amendment for the lands municipally known as 90 Eastdale Avenue and 2 Secord Avenue. As part of Council’s decision, recommendation 1 directed that the draft zoning by-law be revised to increase the maximum building height to 41 storeys, along with associated performance standard changes including overall building height, number of units, unit breakdown and gross floor area, and a revised Schedule A to the Zoning By-law Amendment to include the community benefits and legal conveniences. The Bill was withheld pending the applicant entering into an agreement under Section 37(3) of the Planning Act, as it read the day before Section 1 of Schedule 17 to the COVID-19 Economic Recovery Act, 2020 came into force, to secure affordable housing and rental housing commitments, Council’s approval of the associated rental housing demolition application, and resolution of servicing matters.

The draft Zoning By-law Amendment has been revised in accordance with Council’s direction. The applicant has requested a revision to the draft Zoning By-law Amendment to facilitate the delegated payment-in-lieu of bike parking program process. This process is delegated to staff for sites within City-wide By-law 569-2013, however the zoning for this site remains subject to the former East York Zoning By-law so additional recommendations are required to enable the delegated process in this instance.

Reason for Urgency:

This matter is urgent and time sensitive as the revisions directed by City Council include affordable housing obligations in Schedule A of the zoning by-law, and the updates to cash in lieu of bike parking requirements will allow for expedited implementation.
2026.MM43.133.r:
Councillor Brad Bradford, seconded by Councillor James Pasternak, recommends that:

1. City Council amend its previous decision on Item 2025.TE19.9 by amending recommendation 1, deleting the words “Attachment 5 to the report (December 18, 2024) from the Director, Community Planning, Toronto and East York District” and replacing with the words “Attachment 1”, so that recommendation 1 reads as follows:

1. City Council amend former East York Zoning By-law 6752 and Zoning By-law 958-2020 (LPAT) for the lands municipally known as 90 Eastdale Avenue and 2 Secord Avenue substantially in accordance with the draft Zoning By-law Amendment included as Attachment 1.

2. City Council amend its previous decision on Item 2025.TE19.9 by adding new Recommendations:

6. City Council delegate approval and signing authority to the Executive Director, Development Review for agreements related to payments-in-lieu of bicycle parking under the draft Zoning By-law Amendment referred to in Recommendation 1 in a form satisfactory to the City Solicitor.

7. City Council direct the Executive Director, Development Review to use $552, per short-term bicycle parking space reduced, adjusted for inflation, as the basis upon which payments under the draft Zoning By-law Amendment referred to in Recommendation 1 be calculated.

8. City Council direct the Executive Director, Development Review to use $1103, per long-term bicycle parking space reduced, adjusted for inflation, as the basis upon which payments under the Zoning By-law Amendment referred to in Recommendation 1 be calculated.

9. City Council authorize the City Solicitor to make such changes to the Zoning By-law Amendment and to take any necessary steps to implement City Council's decision.

3. City Council determine that, Pursuant to Section 34(17) of the Planning Act, no further notice is required in respect of the changes to the Zoning By-law Amendment.

2026.MM43.134.t: Strengthening Protections for Homebuyers - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Parthi Kandavel
2026.MM43.134.s:
There have been recent reports in the community of residents purchasing new builds from malicious developers posing as owner-builders to circumvent Government of Ontario regulations. This has led to residents living in unsafe conditions that have caused health and safety concerns, along with financial hardship.

This motion requests the Chief Building Official and the Chief Communications Officer, in consultation with the Home Construction Regulatory Authority and Tarion, to develop a public awareness strategy to educate prospective homebuyers about the risks associated with owner-builder homes, including bad-faith or malicious owner-builder practices. The motion also calls on the Government of Ontario to review the existing regulatory framework governing owner-builders and implement legislative, regulatory, and enforcement measures to close regulatory gaps, deter abuse of the owner-builder exemption, and enhance protections for homebuyers.

Reason for Urgency: This motion is urgent as it relates to the health and safety of residents.
2026.MM43.134.r:
Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Parthi Kandavel, recommends that:

1. City Council request the Chief Building Official and the Chief Communications Officer, Communications Division, in consultation with the Home Construction Regulatory Authority, and Tarion, to develop and implement a communications and public awareness strategy to address risks associated with owner-builder homes, including bad-faith or malicious owner-builder practices, by the third quarter of 2027.

2. City Council request the Province of Ontario to undertake a review of the regulatory framework governing owner-builders and implement legislative, regulatory, and enforcement measures, as appropriate, to address bad-faith or malicious owner-builder practices and strengthen protections for homebuyers.

2026.MM43.135.t: Toronto Needs Container-Friendly Trees as an Option - by Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe
2026.MM43.135.s:
Residents of Willowdale continue to feel discouraged by the state of planters lining Yonge Street, an important economic corridor in our city, home to the largest concentration of office towers outside the downtown core. Currently, a large majority of planters are filled with weeds. This cannot continue, especially as the timeline for Transform Yonge remains unclear. This motion supports the continued work on 2026.MM42.36, in particular, the need for a wider range of tree options to allow for better survivability in older planters. This also moves us closer to a beautiful city!

Reason for Urgency:

This matter is urgent because staff are already carrying out the work for MM42.36 and this motion will supplement and give further direction to that important work.
2026.MM43.135.r:
Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe, recommends that:

1. City Council direct the Executive Director, Environment, Climate and Forestry, in consultation with other appropriate divisions, to include as part of the report back requested under MM42.36 - Public Realm Planters on Yonge Street: Interim Management and Long-Term Governance, steps that can be taken to maintain planters and tree wells along Yonge Street from Sheppard Avenue to Finch Avenue, including:

a. a review and analysis of options to increase the survivability of trees planted in different types of street tree planting infrastructure, including consideration of additional tree species beyond those currently planted by the city; and

b. a review and analysis of options to increase the survivability of developer-planted trees.

2. City Council direct the Executive Director, Environment, Climate and Forestry to inform the local Councillor if deferring any tree replacements within street tree planting infrastructure due to major construction conflicts for an extended period of time.

2026.MM43.136.t: Granting Members of Council Access to all Toronto Parking Authority Board Meeting Materials - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata
2026.MM43.136.s:
At its meeting on November 12 and 13, 2025, City Council amended the composition of the Toronto Parking Authority Board to be composed entirely of City staff.

A consequence of this new board structure, no Members of Council have access to the confidential materials of the Toronto Parking Authority Board.

In order for Council to be able to exercise oversight of the Toronto Parking Authority Board during this interim board structure, Council should allow Members of Council to access all Toronto Parking Authority Board material, including the confidential attachments.

Reason for Urgency:

This matter is urgent because Members of Council require access to the Toronto Parking Authority Board materials and this is the last regular meeting of Council term.
2026.MM43.136.r:
Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata, recommends that:

1. City Council amend Toronto Municipal Code Chapter 179, Parking Authority, to provide that access to confidential Toronto Parking Authority board documents be granted to Members of City Council, upon request, until such time as a new board structure is established by City Council that includes Members of Council.

2026.MM43.138.t: Reimbursement for Works Associated with a New Street Connection of Olympic Garden Drive to Yonge Street - by Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe
2026.MM43.138.s:
As part of a plan of subdivision application for the lands at 5799 Yonge Street, a new public road (Olympic Garden Drive) was approved through the lands connecting Cummer Avenue to the north, and Yonge Street in the southwest part of the site, at the intersection of Yonge Street and Narges Drive. The design, construction, and applicable restoration of the road was secured through the executed subdivision agreement.

To facilitate the construction of the Olympic Garden Drive, a portion of the adjacent lands municipally known as 5795 Yonge Street was acquired by the City, as authorized by City Council. Development charge credits were previously authorized in respect of the land acquisition costs associated with the expropriation.

The acquisition of lands required for the road connection also necessitates the relocation and reconstruction of certain existing access, service and utility infrastructure serving 5795 Yonge Street. These works are required to accommodate the construction of Olympic Garden Drive and restore access and servicing impacted by the road project.

In the normal delivery of a City road project, such relocation and reconstruction works would generally form part of the road construction costs required to deliver the infrastructure project. The subdivision agreement (as per Attachment 1) includes provisions related to potential development charge credits for certain road, water and sewer infrastructure works associated with the development. The works that are the subject of this motion relate exclusively to the road project and associated impacts arriving the from acquisition of land required for Olympic Garden Drive. No water or sewer development charges credits are being requested or provided.

This motion seeks Council authority to provide development charge credits for eligible road-related costs directly attributable to the relocation or reconstruction of services, utilities, access and related works required as a result of the acquisition of lands necessary to complete Olympic Garden Drive. All other costs associated with the development and construction of Olympic Garden Drive, including the signalization of the intersection and other works required to service the development, remain the responsibility of the developer.

Reason for Urgency:

This Motion is urgent as the July 29 to 31, 2026 meeting represents the final opportunity for City Council to provide the necessary authority to facilitate the timely completion of Olympic Garden Drive and its connection to Cummer Ave before the commencement of the Council recess and election period.

Absent Council's authorization at this time, the project may experience significant delays, resulting in the continued closure of the roadway connection, deferred public benefits, and potential impacts to traffic in the community. Advancing this Motion will provide certainty to all parties, enable staff to proceed with the reimbursement framework contemplated through the Subdivision Agreement, and support the timely delivery of a public asset that has already been approved by Council and secured through the development approvals process.
2026.MM43.138.r:
Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Dianne Saxe, recommends that:

1. City Council approve a development charge credit against the Roads component of development charges for the eligible road-related costs associated with the relocation or reconstruction of services, utilities, access and related works required to facilitate construction of Olympic Garden Drive and arising from the acquisition of land required for the road connection, with eligible expenses to be determined to the satisfaction of the Director, Engineering Review, Development Review, and to the satisfaction of the General Manager of Transportation Services. The development charge credit shall be in an amount that is the lesser of the cost to the Owner of eligible works noted above, as approved by the Director, Engineering Review, Development Review and to the satisfaction of the General Manager of Transportation Services, and the Roads component of development charges payable for the development in accordance with the City's Development Charges By-law, as may be amended from time to time, net of any credits previously provided for the land expropriation.

2. City Council authorize the Executive Director, Development Review, in consultation with the General Manager, Transportation Services and the City Solicitor, to negotiate and execute any agreements, amendments to existing agreements, and ancillary documents required to implement the development charge credits authorized by this motion, including provisions respecting the determination of eligible costs, documentation requirements, timing and manner in which development charges credits may be provided, and any other terms and conditions deemed appropriate by the Executive Director, Development Review and the City Solicitor, including provisions of development charges credits in phases tied to project milestones, including but not limited to the completion of design, construction works and the connection of the new street to Cummer Avenue.
